units.title: HELLO, WHO ARE YOU?
units.theme: Introducing yourself, your name and your people

overview.intro: This first unit gives you the words you will use every single day: your name, where you are from, and who the people around you are. Everything is built on one small verb — “to be” — plus the little words that show who owns what (my, your, his, her).
goals: Say who you are and ask other people who they are.
Use am, is and are correctly with I, you, he, she, it, we and they.
Use my, your, his, her, our and their to talk about your family and your things.
overview.outcome: By the end you can introduce yourself in five sentences and ask a classmate four questions about who they are.

vocab.def: the word people use to call you.
vocab.use: We say “My name is Ana” or “I am Ana”. Never both together: not “My name is I am Ana”.
examples: My name is Carlos.
What is your name?
vocab.colloc: first name · last name · full name

vocab.def: a person you like and spend time with.
vocab.use: Add “my” before it when you talk about your own friend: “my friend Sara”.
examples: This is my friend Sara.
We are good friends.
vocab.colloc: a good friend · a best friend · my friend from school

vocab.def: a place like Colombia, Mexico or Canada.
vocab.use: With countries we use “from”: “I am from Colombia.”
examples: What country are you from?
My country is beautiful.
vocab.colloc: my country · a big country · from another country

vocab.def: a person who studies at a school or university.
vocab.use: Use “a” before it in the singular: “I am a student.” Do not forget the “a”.
examples: I am a student at the university.
They are students in my class.
vocab.colloc: a good student · a new student · a student of English

vocab.def: kind, pleasant, easy to like.
vocab.use: Very common in greetings: “Nice to meet you.” Also for people and things.
examples: Nice to meet you, Mr Lopez.
Your teacher is very nice.
vocab.colloc: nice to meet you · a nice person · really nice

vocab.def: your parents, brothers, sisters and relatives.
vocab.use: “Family” is one word for the whole group, so we usually say “My family is big.”
examples: My family is not very big.
Is this your family?
vocab.colloc: a big family · a small family · my whole family

vocab.def: to come from a place — your city or country.
vocab.use: Always “be” + “from”: “I am from Cali.” Never “I have from Cali” and never without “from”.
examples: Where are you from?
She is from Ecuador, and her husband is from Peru.
vocab.colloc: be from Colombia · originally from · where are you from

vocab.def: having a husband or wife / having no husband or wife.
vocab.use: With “to be”, not “have”: “I am married.” The person is “married to” someone: “She is married to Luis.”
examples: My brother is married.
Are you single or married?
vocab.colloc: happily married · married to · still single

vocab.def: a person who lives near you.
vocab.use: “My neighbour” is one person; “my neighbours” is the family or the people around you. US spelling: neighbor.
examples: My neighbour is a doctor.
Our neighbours are very friendly.
vocab.colloc: a good neighbour · next-door neighbour

vocab.def: the work you do to earn money.
vocab.use: Countable, so it needs “a”: “I have a job”, “She is a nurse”. “Work” is uncountable: “I have a lot of work.”
examples: What is your job?
He has a new job in a hotel.
vocab.colloc: a good job · a part-time job · look for a job

vocab.def: a short or friendly name people use instead of your real name.
vocab.use: Say “My nickname is…”. The verb is “to call”: “Everyone calls me Pipe.”
examples: My name is Felipe, but my nickname is Pipe.
Do you have a nickname at home?
vocab.colloc: a nickname · my nickname is · they call me

vocab.def: not married / married.
vocab.use: Both go after “to be”: “I am single.” Never with “have”.
examples: My sister is married and she has two children.
I’m single and I live with my parents.
vocab.colloc: be single · be married to someone

grammar.name: Verb “to be” + possessive adjectives
grammar.short: I am, you are, he is + my, your, his, her.
grammar.rule: “To be” has three forms in the present: am (with I), is (with he, she, it) and are (with you, we, they). Possessive adjectives — my, your, his, her, its, our, their — go in front of a noun to show who it belongs to.
form: I am / You are / He is / She is / It is / We are / They are.
Short forms: I’m, you’re, he’s, she’s, it’s, we’re, they’re.
my book · your teacher · his sister · her name · our class · their house.
notes: Always use a subject: “She is my sister”, never “Is my sister”.
Possessive adjectives never change with plurals: “my books”, not “mys books”.
“His” is for a man and “her” is for a woman — it follows the owner, not the object: “Ana and her brother”, “Luis and his sister”.
examples: I am Ana and this is my brother.
She is our English teacher.
They are students. Their class is at nine.
grammar.watch: Do not confuse “his” (of a man) with “her” (of a woman): “Mario and her mother” is wrong — say “his mother”.
grammar.deep: “To be” is the smallest verb in English and the busiest. It does three different jobs: it links a subject to a name (I am Ana), to a description (she is tired), and to a place (we are at home). Because it is so frequent, English never allows you to leave it out — a sentence like “She my sister” has no verb at all, even though many languages accept it. The three forms exist for historical reasons and there is no logic to learn, only a pattern to automate: am belongs to I alone, is belongs to the three singular people and things, and are covers everything else. Possessive adjectives sit in front of the noun and never change shape, no matter how many things you own, because English marks the plural on the noun and nowhere else: my book, my books, my brother’s books.

To show who owns something, add ’s to the person.

drill.name: Chain of three
drill.prompt: Say three sentences about one person: name, relationship, one detail. Change person and repeat.
items: This is Sofía. She is my sister. Her hair is very long.
That is Camilo. He is my classmate. His English is good.
Now use: my mother — her job.
Now use: my friends — their city.
Now use: my dog — its name.

grammar.name: Wh-questions and yes/no questions with “to be”
grammar.short: Who are you? Are you a student? Yes, I am.
grammar.rule: To make a question with “to be”, put the verb before the subject. For yes/no questions start with am/is/are; for open questions start with a wh-word (who, what, where, how old).
form: Am/Is/Are + subject + …? → Are you Colombian?
Wh-word + am/is/are + subject? → Where is your school?
Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, she isn’t. / Yes, they are.
notes: Never use “do” with “to be”: “Are you a student?”, not “Do you are a student?”.
In short answers with “yes” we do not use the short form: “Yes, I am”, not “Yes, I’m”.
“How old are you?” uses “to be” in English — not “have”.
examples: Where are you from?
Is he your friend? — No, he isn’t.
How old is your sister? — She is twelve.
grammar.watch: The answer to “Are you…?” is about you: “Are you tired?” — “Yes, I am.” Change the person in the answer.
grammar.deep: English marks a question in one of two ways, and “to be” uses the older one: it simply swaps places with the subject. “You are ready” becomes “Are you ready?” with no extra word at all, which is why adding “do” to a “to be” question is such a visible error — the sentence already contains its own question marker. Two habits will keep your answers natural. First, always give the short answer with the same verb form that appeared in the question, changing the person: “Are you tired?” — “Yes, I am.” Second, never contract a positive short answer: “Yes, I am” is correct, “Yes, I’m” is not, because English will not end a sentence on a contraction. In the negative you have the opposite freedom: “No, I’m not” and “No, I am not” are both fine.

drill.name: Three questions, three answers
drill.prompt: Ask your partner and write the short answer only.

dialogue.line: Are you new here?
Yes, I am. I’m from Pasto.
Where is Pasto exactly?
In the south. Is your family from Bogotá?
No, they aren’t. They’re from Santa Marta.

grammar.sound: Yes/no questions go UP at the end (Are you a student↗). Wh-questions go DOWN (Where are you from↘).

speaking.text: Introduce yourself to three classmates: name, country, job or studies. Then say one thing about your family.
Stand in a circle. Ask the person on your right one “to be” question. They answer, then ask the next person a different question.
You meet a new student at the door of the class. Greet them and find out four things about them.

tips: Remember the contraction: “I’m”, “you’re”, “he’s” — it sounds much more natural than the long form.
Use “a” before jobs: “She is a doctor”, not “She is doctor”.
Capital letters for countries, languages and names: Colombia, Spanish, Ana.

quiz.explain: “Name” is singular, so we use “is”: “Is your name Miguel?”

dynamics.name: Name chain
dynamics.how: Student 1 says “I’m Ana.” Student 2 says “She is Ana and I’m Luis.” Each student repeats everyone before them. When somebody breaks, the chain restarts from that student.
dynamics.payoff: Forces he/she and is/am into automatic use, and everybody learns the names.

dynamics.name: Two truths, one lie
dynamics.how: Each student writes three sentences about their family with “my / his / her”. One is false. The group asks two yes/no questions each before voting on the lie.
dynamics.payoff: Yes/no questions and possessives in the same activity, with a reason to listen.

dynamics.name: Who is who?
dynamics.how: Student A describes four people in a family photo (real or drawn) without pointing. Student B numbers them on the paper and then reads the numbers back.
dynamics.payoff: Practises “This is…, He is…, Her name is…” with a checkable result.

dynamics.name: Mingle bingo
dynamics.how: Give a 3×3 grid: “is 18 years old”, “is from another city”, “has a nickname”… Students ask full questions to fill a name in each square. No square may repeat a name.
dynamics.payoff: Twenty repetitions of “Are you…? / Is your…?” in ten minutes.

writing.title: My people, in six lines
writing.brief: Write six sentences: your name, where you are from, your age, one family member, that person’s name and one detail about them. Use a possessive adjective in at least four sentences.
criteria: Every sentence has a form of “to be”.
At least four different possessives (my, your, his, her, our, their).
Ages use “is / am” + “years old”.

homework.title: Voice note: introduce three people
homework.task: Record a 45-second voice note introducing yourself and two people at home. Say each person’s name, relationship and one detail. Listen back once and re-record if you hear “I have 20 years” or a missing “is”.

test.explain: “Name” is singular, so the question starts with “Is”.
Mario is a man, so the possessive is “his”.
“Brothers” is plural, so we use “are”.
Short answers use the full form: “Yes, I am.”
“Where” asks about place.

units.title: MY DAY, MY ROUTINE
units.theme: Daily habits and telling people when things happen

overview.intro: This unit is about your normal day: what you do, when you do it, and how often. You will meet the present simple with “do” and “does”, and the small words that put an action on the clock or the calendar — at, in, on, before, after, until.
goals: Ask and answer questions about daily routines with do and does.
Add -s or -es correctly when you talk about he, she or it.
Use time expressions to say exactly when something happens.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe your whole day in order and ask a partner five questions about theirs.

vocab.def: to stop sleeping.
vocab.use: “Wake up” is opening your eyes; “get up” is leaving the bed. We often use both together.
examples: I wake up at six and get up at six thirty.
What time do you wake up?
vocab.colloc: wake up early · wake up late · wake up at seven

vocab.def: the first meal of the day.
vocab.use: We say “have breakfast”, not “take breakfast”. No “the” before it.
examples: I have breakfast with my mother.
She never has breakfast before work.
vocab.colloc: have breakfast · a big breakfast · before breakfast

vocab.def: every time, one hundred per cent of the time.
vocab.use: It goes before the main verb: “I always study at night.” But after “to be”: “He is always late.”
examples: I always drink coffee in the morning.
My brother is always tired on Mondays.
vocab.colloc: always late · almost always · always the same

vocab.def: to end something, to arrive at the last part.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or by -ing: “finish work”, “finish eating”.
examples: I finish work at five o’clock.
We finish studying and then we watch TV.
vocab.colloc: finish work · finish class · finish early

vocab.def: Saturday and Sunday.
vocab.use: With days and dates we use “on”: “on the weekend” (US) or “at the weekend” (UK).
examples: On the weekend I visit my grandmother.
What do you do on weekends?
vocab.colloc: on the weekend · every weekend · a long weekend

vocab.def: before the normal time / after the normal time.
vocab.use: They come after the verb: “I get up early”, “She arrives late”. Never “I early get up”.
examples: I go to bed early on Sundays.
He always arrives late to class.
vocab.colloc: very early · too late · early in the morning

vocab.def: to get out of bed.
vocab.use: Different from “wake up”: you wake up first (eyes open), then you get up (leave the bed).
examples: I get up at six thirty every day.
On Sundays I get up late.
vocab.colloc: get up early · get up late · what time do you get up

vocab.def: most of the time, but not always.
vocab.use: It goes before the main verb and after “to be”: “I usually work at home”, “She is usually late”.
examples: I usually take the bus to work.
We usually have lunch at one.
vocab.colloc: usually work · not usually · as usual

vocab.def: to use transport; to need an amount of time.
vocab.use: “Take the bus / the metro / a taxi” for transport, and “it takes + time” for duration: “It takes me an hour.”
examples: I take the metro every morning.
It takes twenty minutes to get to work.
vocab.colloc: take the bus · take a taxi · it takes time

vocab.def: the midday meal / the evening meal.
vocab.use: With “have”, and with no article: “have lunch at one”, “after dinner”. Never “take lunch”.
examples: I have lunch at work.
We have dinner together every night.
vocab.colloc: have lunch · before dinner · a quick lunch

vocab.def: Monday to Friday / Saturday and Sunday.
vocab.use: Use “on weekdays” and “at the weekend” (British) or “on the weekend” (American).
examples: On weekdays I start work at eight.
At the weekend I sleep until nine.
vocab.colloc: on weekdays · at the weekend · every weekend

grammar.name: Present simple wh-questions with do/does
grammar.short: What do you do? Where does she work?
grammar.rule: For habits and routines we use the present simple. Questions need the helper “do” (I, you, we, they) or “does” (he, she, it). With he/she/it in statements the verb takes -s or -es.
form: Wh-word + do/does + subject + verb? → Where do you live?
Do/Does + subject + verb? → Does he study English?
Statement: He works. She watches TV. It finishes at six.
notes: After “does”, the main verb has no -s: “Does she work?”, not “Does she works?”.
Spelling: add -es after -ch, -sh, -ss, -x, -o (watches, finishes, goes); “study” becomes “studies”.
“Have” becomes “has”: “She has two brothers.”
examples: What time do you start work?
Where does your brother study?
He goes to the gym and watches a film after dinner.
grammar.watch: The -s goes in ONE place only — on the verb in a statement, or on “does” in a question. Never both.
grammar.deep: The present simple is the tense of things that are generally true: routines, habits, timetables and facts. Its only real difficulty is a single letter. In the third person singular — he, she, it, and any name or singular noun — the verb takes -s, and everywhere else it stays bare. English also insists that this marking appears exactly once per sentence, which is the key to questions: as soon as the helper “does” carries the -s, the main verb must go back to its base form. That is why “Does she works?” feels wrong to a native ear — the sentence is marked twice. Build your questions in the fixed order wh-word, helper, subject, verb, and the structure will hold together: “Where does your brother work?”

drill.prompt: Change the sentence from “I” to “my brother” and say it aloud.

Does she take the bus?

grammar.name: Time expressions
grammar.short: at, around, early, late, until, before, after, on, in.
grammar.rule: Small words put your actions on the clock and the calendar. Each one has its own job, and English keeps them very fixed.
form: at + clock time: at seven, at midnight. around + approximate time: around eight.
on + day or date: on Monday, on 5 May. in + month, year, part of day: in July, in the morning.
before / after + time or action: before class, after lunch. until + the end point: until ten.
notes: “At night” is the exception — not “in the night”.
“Early” and “late” are not nouns: say “early in the morning”, not “in the early morning” at this level.
“Until” marks where something stops: “I work until six” means six is the end.
examples: I start work at eight and stay until five.
On Saturdays I get up around ten.
She studies in the evening, after dinner.
grammar.watch: Do not use “in” with clock times: “at three o’clock”, never “in three o’clock”.
grammar.deep: Time prepositions look tiny but they carry a whole system, and English fixes them so firmly that a wrong one is heard immediately. The cleanest way to hold them in your head is by size of the container. “At” goes with the smallest, sharpest points of time — a clock hour, midnight, noon. “On” goes with a whole day or date, which is a bigger box. “In” goes with the biggest boxes: months, seasons, years, and the broad parts of the day. The famous exception, “at night”, is worth learning as a single word rather than a rule. Around this core sit the sequencing words: before and after put your action next to another event, and until marks the point where something stops, so “I work until six” tells your listener where the activity ends, not how long it lasted.

speaking.text: Tell your partner your Monday, hour by hour. Your partner writes the times and repeats your day back to you.
Ask four classmates: What time do you wake up? When do you study? What do you do on the weekend? Report the most common answers.
You are a doctor asking a patient about their daily routine. Ask about food, sleep and exercise.

tips: Say the -s clearly on he/she/it — it is the number-one A1 mistake.
“Do” and “does” never take -s together with the verb: “Does he live…?”
Keep the order: at + hour, on + day, in + month.

quiz.q: What time ___ your sister leave home?
quiz.explain: “Your sister” is he/she/it, so the helper is “does”, and “leave” stays in the base form.

dynamics.name: Routine race
dynamics.how: Partner A reads their day out of order (“I have dinner… I wake up…”). Partner B writes it in the right order and reads it back using “you”. Then swap.
dynamics.payoff: Time expressions get used for a real purpose — reordering.

dynamics.name: Find the imposter
dynamics.how: Each student writes five sentences about their weekday routine; one is invented. The group asks “Do you…? / What time do you…?” until they vote.
dynamics.payoff: Do/does questions with a reason to ask them.

dynamics.name: Clock dictation
dynamics.how: Read eight times and activities quickly (“at quarter past six, breakfast”). Students draw the clock hands and write the activity, then compare in pairs.
dynamics.payoff: Trains the ear for the time patterns learners mishear most.

dynamics.name: Family reporter
dynamics.how: Each student reports one family member’s routine in the third person. The group counts the -s endings out loud and corrects anything missing.
dynamics.payoff: Puts the -s under public pressure, which is what makes it stick.

writing.title: A weekday and a weekend day
writing.brief: Write two short paragraphs: your usual Tuesday and your usual Sunday. Use at least five different time expressions and mention one other person’s routine in the third person.
criteria: Every he/she verb in a statement has -s or -es.
At least five different time expressions (at, on, in, before, after, until).
Questions, if any, use do / does correctly.

homework.title: Interview somebody at home
homework.task: Ask a family member five present-simple questions about their day and write their answers in the third person (“She gets up at…”). Underline every -s you added.

test.q: What time ___ your sister leave home?
test.explain: “Your sister” is he/she/it, so the helper is “does” and the verb stays in the base form.
Verbs ending in -ch add -es: watches.
Days take “on”.
Clock times take “at”.
“They” takes “do”.

units.title: THIS, THAT AND BETTER
units.theme: Pointing at things and comparing them

overview.intro: In this unit you learn to point: this shirt here, that shop over there, these shoes, those people. Then you learn to compare — which one is cheaper, bigger, more comfortable, more expensive.
goals: Choose between this, that, these and those depending on number and distance.
Form comparatives with short adjectives (-er) and long adjectives (more).
Compare two things in a shop, a street or a photo.
overview.outcome: By the end you can go shopping in English, point at three items and say which one is better and why.

vocab.def: costing little money / costing a lot of money.
vocab.use: Things are cheap or expensive, not prices. Say “The shirt is expensive”, not “The price is expensive”.
examples: This bag is cheap, but that one is very expensive.
Is the restaurant expensive?
vocab.colloc: really cheap · too expensive · cheaper than

vocab.def: how big or small something is; also clothes measurement.
vocab.use: In shops: “What size are you?” “I’m a medium.”
examples: Do you have this shirt in a bigger size?
What size are your shoes?
vocab.colloc: a big size · the same size · size medium

vocab.def: to put clothes on in a shop to see if they fit.
vocab.use: Separable: “try it on”, not “try on it”, when you use a pronoun.
examples: Can I try on these jeans?
I like that jacket — I want to try it on.
vocab.colloc: try on a shirt · try it on · try them on

vocab.def: pleasant to wear, sit in or use.
vocab.use: It is a long adjective, so the comparative is “more comfortable”, never “comfortabler”.
examples: These shoes are more comfortable than those.
The old sofa is very comfortable.
vocab.colloc: very comfortable · more comfortable than · comfortable shoes

vocab.def: full of people.
vocab.use: Used for places, not people: “The market is crowded”, not “The people are crowded”.
examples: This shop is crowded on Saturdays.
The bus is more crowded in the morning.
vocab.colloc: a crowded market · very crowded · too crowded

vocab.def: the word that joins the two things you compare.
vocab.use: Always after the comparative: “bigger than”, “more expensive than”. Not “bigger that”.
examples: My city is smaller than yours.
This café is nicer than that one.
vocab.colloc: bigger than · better than · more than

vocab.def: a way of pointing without repeating the noun.
vocab.use: Use “one” for a countable thing you have already named: “I like this one better than that one.”
examples: Which one do you prefer, this one or that one?
These are nice, but I want those ones.
vocab.colloc: this one · that one over there · which one

vocab.def: to have a price.
vocab.use: “How much does it cost?” The thing costs; the person pays: “The shirt costs 40,000 pesos.”
examples: How much do these shoes cost?
It costs more than I expected.
vocab.colloc: cost a lot · how much does it cost · cost less

vocab.def: the irregular comparatives of good and bad.
vocab.use: Never “more good” or “gooder”. Keep “than” after them: “better than”, “worse than”.
examples: This café is better than the one near my house.
The traffic is worse in the morning.
vocab.colloc: much better · a bit worse · better than nothing

vocab.def: not weighing much / weighing a lot.
vocab.use: Short adjectives, so the comparatives are “lighter” and “heavier”. Also used for meals and rain.
examples: This bag is lighter than mine.
The box is too heavy for one person.
vocab.colloc: very light · a bit heavier · heavy rain

vocab.def: something you buy much cheaper than its normal price.
vocab.use: “It’s a bargain” is a whole comment on a price. The adjective is “cheap”, not “bargain”.
examples: Two shirts for 40,000 pesos — that’s a bargain.
I found a real bargain at the market.
vocab.colloc: a real bargain · a good bargain · bargain prices

grammar.name: Demonstratives: this, that, these, those
grammar.short: Near or far, one or many.
grammar.rule: Demonstratives point at things. “This/these” are for things near you; “that/those” are for things far from you. “This/that” are singular; “these/those” are plural.
form: Singular near: this shirt. Singular far: that shirt.
Plural near: these shoes. Plural far: those shoes.
Alone as a pronoun: “This is my bag.” “Those are expensive.”
notes: Use “this” on the phone to say who you are: “Hello, this is Ana.”
“One / ones” avoids repeating the noun: “I like this one”, “Those ones are cheaper”.
With plural demonstratives the verb is plural: “These are nice”, not “These is nice”.
examples: This jacket is nice, but that one is cheaper.
These are my books; those are yours.
How much are those shoes?
grammar.watch: “These” (plural, long sound) and “this” (singular, short sound) are easy to confuse — check if the noun ends in -s.
grammar.deep: Demonstratives are English’s pointing fingers, and they carry exactly two pieces of information: how many things, and how far away. Near and singular gives this, near and plural gives these; far and singular gives that, far and plural gives those. Notice that distance is not only physical — English also uses “that” for something the other person mentioned, or something in the past, which is why “that idea” often sounds slightly distant even in writing. One thing to watch: demonstratives work both as determiners in front of a noun (this shirt) and as pronouns standing alone (this is expensive). When you need to stand alone but keep the noun idea alive, add “one”: “I’ll take this one.” That little word is what stops you repeating the noun in every sentence of a shopping conversation.
more: This jacket is nice, but that one is cheaper.
These shoes are too small — do you have those in a bigger size?
Is this your bag or that one?
Those people over there are waiting for the bus.
I like these, but I don’t like those.
How much is this? And how much are these?

fix.why: “Shoes” is plural, so the demonstrative must be plural too.
“Look” needs “at” before the thing you look at.
Plural noun → “those” + “are”.

drill.name: Near or far, one or many
drill.prompt: Point and say the full sentence with the right word.
items: ___ is my chair (the one you touch)

dialogue.line: How much is this shirt?
That one is 60,000. These over here are cheaper.
And those jeans at the back?
Those are the most expensive ones, sorry.

grammar.sound: “This” is short /ɪ/; “these” is long /iː/. Say the pair ten times: this–these, this–these.

grammar.name: Comparatives with short and long adjectives
grammar.short: cheaper than / more expensive than.
grammar.rule: To compare two things we change the adjective. Short adjectives (one syllable, and two ending in -y) add -er. Longer adjectives use “more” in front. Then we add “than” before the second thing.
form: Short: cheap → cheaper, big → bigger, easy → easier.
Long: expensive → more expensive, comfortable → more comfortable.
Irregular: good → better, bad → worse, far → further.
notes: Double the final consonant after one short vowel: big → bigger, hot → hotter, thin → thinner.
-y becomes -ier: happy → happier, busy → busier, easy → easier.
Never mix the two systems: “more cheaper” is always wrong.
examples: Bogotá is bigger than Cartagena.
This phone is more expensive than mine.
Today is better than yesterday.
grammar.watch: Use “than”, not “that” or “to”, after a comparative: “taller than me”.
grammar.deep: Comparatives split adjectives into two families by length, and the rule is about syllables rather than meaning. One-syllable adjectives, and two-syllable ones ending in -y, add -er: cheaper, bigger, easier. Everything longer takes “more” in front: more expensive, more comfortable, more interesting. There is no overlap — “more cheap” and “expensiver” are both broken — and the small irregular group (good/better, bad/worse, far/further) simply has to be memorised. The second half of the structure is “than”, which introduces the thing you are comparing with and cannot be replaced by “that”. If you want to strengthen the comparison, put an intensifier before it: “much cheaper”, “a lot more comfortable”, “a bit better”. Those intensifiers are what make a comparison sound like an opinion rather than a measurement.

rows: good → better, bad → worse, far → further

more: This bag is cheaper than that one.
The blue shirt is more expensive than the white one.
My phone is better than my old one.
Bogotá is colder than Cartagena.
These jeans are more comfortable than those.
Today is worse than yesterday.

fix.why: Short adjectives take -er, never “more”.

fix.wrong: She is more tall that me.
fix.why: Two errors: -er for short adjectives, and “than” for comparison.
“Good” is irregular: good → better.

drill.name: Make it comparative
drill.prompt: Compare the two things aloud in one sentence.

dialogue.line: Which one do you like more?
The grey one — it’s cheaper and more comfortable than the black one.
But the black one is better quality, isn’t it?
Yes, but it’s much more expensive.

grammar.sound: “Than” is unstressed and almost disappears: “cheaper thən this”. Never stress it.

Compare your two favourite places in your city: which is bigger, cheaper, more beautiful, more crowded?
One student describes an object in the room using a comparative (“It is smaller than the door”). The others guess it.

tips: Count the syllables: one syllable → -er; three or more → more.
“This” and “these” for what you can touch; “that” and “those” for what is across the room.
“Good” and “bad” are irregular: better, worse — never “gooder”.

quiz.explain: “Comfortable” is a long adjective, so the comparative is “more comfortable than”.

dynamics.payoff: Demonstratives and comparatives in one natural exchange.

dynamics.how: Show two similar photos. Students write five differences using comparatives, then read them to another pair, who must guess which photo is which.
dynamics.payoff: Forces precise comparison instead of single adjectives.

“Than” appears after every comparative.
Demonstratives agree with singular or plural nouns.

units.title: ASKING AND OFFERING
units.theme: Questions, object pronouns and polite offers

overview.intro: This unit is about talking with people, not just about them. You will practise asking full questions, replacing names with object pronouns (me, you, him, her, us, them), and making polite offers and invitations with “would”.
goals: Form wh-questions and yes/no questions in the present simple confidently.
Replace nouns with the correct object pronoun.
Offer and invite politely with Would you like…?
overview.outcome: By the end you can order in a café, invite a friend somewhere and answer a polite offer correctly.

vocab.def: to ask someone to come somewhere with you.
vocab.use: Pattern: invite + person + to + place/event: “She invited me to her party.”
examples: I want to invite you to dinner.
They invited us to the wedding.
vocab.colloc: invite a friend · invite someone to a party

vocab.def: to ask for food or drink in a restaurant.
vocab.use: Also a noun: “Can I take your order?”
examples: I would like to order a coffee, please.
Are you ready to order?
vocab.colloc: order food · order a drink · take an order

vocab.def: the two words that make any request polite.
vocab.use: “Please” goes at the end of a request or right after “can”. “Thank you” answers a favour or an offer.
examples: Two teas, please.
Thank you very much — that’s very kind.
vocab.colloc: yes please · no thank you · thanks a lot

vocab.def: not busy; also costing no money.
vocab.use: For time: “Are you free tomorrow?” For money: “The museum is free on Sundays.”
examples: Are you free on Friday evening?
The entrance is free for students.
vocab.colloc: free time · free on Saturday · completely free

vocab.def: to come together with someone at a place and time.
vocab.use: “Meet” for the first time, and also for arranging: “Let’s meet at seven.”
examples: Let’s meet in front of the cinema.
I meet my friends every Friday.
vocab.colloc: meet a friend · meet at six · nice to meet you

vocab.def: with each other, in the same place.
vocab.use: It comes at the end of the sentence: “We study together.”
examples: Do you want to go together?
We had lunch together yesterday.
vocab.colloc: work together · go together · all together

vocab.def: to hand something to someone.
vocab.use: Two objects: “give me the book” or “give the book to me”. Never “give to me the book”.
examples: Can you give me your number?
She gave the keys to her brother.
vocab.colloc: give me a hand · give it to her · give an example

vocab.def: to do something useful for someone.
vocab.use: “Help me”, “help her” — the object pronoun comes straight after the verb, with no preposition.
examples: Can you help me with this?
I always help my parents on Saturdays.
vocab.colloc: help me · help with the homework · a big help

vocab.def: a polite way of saying “want”.
vocab.use: Always “would like + to + verb” or “would like + noun”: “I’d like to order”, “I’d like a coffee”. Never “would like + -ing”.
examples: Would you like a drink?
I’d like to see the menu, please.
vocab.colloc: I’d like · would you like · would you like to

vocab.def: perhaps; possibly.
vocab.use: One word at the start of the sentence: “Maybe later.” Two words (“may be”) is a verb: “It may be true.”
examples: Maybe we can meet on Friday.
Maybe not today — I’m busy.
vocab.colloc: maybe later · maybe not · maybe tomorrow

vocab.def: to help someone.
vocab.use: Very common in requests: “Can you give me a hand?” Informal and friendly.
examples: Could you give me a hand with these bags?
She gave us a hand in the kitchen.
vocab.colloc: give somebody a hand · need a hand

vocab.def: take what you want (food or drink) without asking.
vocab.use: An offer, not an order. “Help yourself to the coffee.”
examples: Help yourself to some cake.
Please help yourselves, everybody.
vocab.colloc: help yourself to something

grammar.name: Wh- and yes/no questions + object pronouns
grammar.short: Who does she call? — She calls me.
grammar.rule: Subject pronouns (I, you, he, she, we, they) do the action. Object pronouns (me, you, him, her, it, us, them) receive it, and they go after the verb or after a preposition.
form: Subject → object: I → me, he → him, she → her, we → us, they → them (you and it do not change).
After a verb: “I know her.” After a preposition: “I’m talking to him.”
Questions: Do you know him? · Who do they invite? · Where does she meet them?
notes: Never use a subject pronoun after a verb: “I saw he” is wrong — “I saw him”.
With two objects, the person usually comes first: “Give me the book.”
“Who” asks about people; if the person is the object we still start with “Who”: “Who do you call?”
examples: Do you know her? — Yes, she works with me.
My parents call us every Sunday.
Who does he invite to the party?
grammar.watch: After prepositions always use the object form: “between you and me”, “with him”, “for us”.
grammar.deep: Object pronouns are the second half of a system you already know. Every person has a subject form, which does the action, and an object form, which receives it: I/me, you/you, he/him, she/her, we/us, they/them. English decides which one you need purely by position — before the verb you use the subject form, after the verb or after a preposition you use the object form. That is why “between you and I” is wrong even though it sounds careful: “between” is a preposition, so it must take “me”. Question words follow the same logic, and this is where “who” and “whom” come from, although modern speech uses “who” almost everywhere. Once you can feel the difference between “She called him” and “He called her”, the whole family falls into place.

chart.title: Subject and object pronouns
rows: I called her. / She called me.
You know him. / He knows you.
He helped us. / We helped him.
She invited them. / They invited her.
We saw them. / They saw us.
They like it. / I like them.

more: Do you know her? — Yes, I work with her.
My parents call us every Sunday.
Who does he invite to the party?
I’m talking to him right now.
Can you help me? I can’t find it.
She sent them a message yesterday.

fix.why: After a verb we need the object pronoun.
After a preposition, always the object form.
After “does” the verb has no -s.

drill.name: Replace the name
drill.prompt: Say the sentence again with a pronoun instead of the underlined words.
items: He works with you and me. →
They call my sister and me. →

dialogue.line: Do you know Camila?
Yes, I study with her. Why?
Can you give her this book? I never see her.
Sure, I’ll give it to her tomorrow.

grammar.sound: “Him” and “them” lose their first sound in fast speech: “I saw ’im”, “I called ’em”.

grammar.name: Yes/no questions with “would”
grammar.short: Would you like a coffee? — Yes, please.
grammar.rule: “Would you like…?” is the polite way to offer something or invite someone. “Would” is the same for every person and is followed by the base verb or by “to + verb”.
form: Would you like + noun? → Would you like some water?
Would you like + to + verb? → Would you like to sit here?
Answers: Yes, please. / No, thank you. / I’d love to. / I’d like a tea, please.
notes: “Would you like…?” is an offer; “Do you like…?” asks about a general taste. They are not the same.
The short form of “I would” is “I’d”: “I’d like the chicken.”
After “would like” we never use -ing: “I’d like to go”, not “I’d like going”.
examples: Would you like something to drink?
Would you like to come with us on Saturday?
I’d like a small coffee, please.
grammar.watch: Answer an offer with “Yes, please” or “No, thank you” — “Yes, I want” sounds rude in English.
grammar.deep: “Would” is English’s politeness engine. Grammatically it is a modal, so it takes no -s, needs no “do”, and is always followed by a base verb — which is why “Would you like to come?” has “like” and “come” in their plainest forms. What makes it special is what it does socially: by putting the request one step away from reality, it gives your listener room to say no, and English hears that space as courtesy. Two things are worth automating. First, the answer pattern: a positive reply is normally “Yes, please” or “I’d love to”, not “Yes, I would like”, which sounds mechanical. Second, the difference between “Do you like coffee?” (a question about your tastes in general) and “Would you like a coffee?” (an offer, right now). Mixing those two is the fastest way to confuse a waiter.

chart.title: Would: offers, requests and answers
rows: Would you like to join us?
Would you like dessert? — Yes, please.
No, thank you. / I’d love to, but…

more: Would you like a coffee? — Yes, please.
Would you like to sit here?
Would you like some help with that?
Would you like anything else? — No, thank you.
Would your friends like to come?
I’d like a bottle of water, please.

fix.why: “Do you like” asks about your taste in general; “Would you like” offers something now.

fix.wrong: Would you like to a coffee?
fix.why: “To” only appears before a verb, not before a noun.
“Would like” + to + verb.

drill.name: Offer and answer
drill.prompt: Make the offer, then give a polite answer.

dialogue.line: Would you like something to drink?
Yes, please — I’d like a lemonade.
And would you like to sit outside?
No, thank you. It’s a bit cold.

grammar.sound: “Would you” joins into /ˈwʊdʒə/ (“woodja”), and “I’d like” is one beat.

speaking.text: Waiter and customer in a café. The waiter offers with “Would you like…?”; the customer orders politely.
Invite your partner to three different places. They accept one and refuse two, politely.
Chain game: one student says a sentence with a name; the next student repeats it using an object pronoun.

tips: “Would you like…?” = an offer now. “Do you like…?” = your taste in general.
Object pronouns come after the verb — never before it.
Soften any request with “please” at the end.

quiz.q: That’s my teacher. Do you know ___?
quiz.explain: After the verb “know” we need the object pronoun “her”.

dynamics.name: Pronoun hot potato
dynamics.how: Say a sentence with a name (“I called Ana”). The next student repeats it with a pronoun (“I called her”) and adds a new sentence with a name. Hesitation passes the turn.
dynamics.payoff: Automates the subject/object switch.

dynamics.name: The café
dynamics.how: One waiter, two customers. The waiter must make four “Would you like…?” offers; customers must refuse two politely and ask one question with a pronoun. Then rotate roles.
dynamics.payoff: Polite offers in the situation where they actually happen.

dynamics.name: Favour chain
dynamics.how: Each student gets a card with a small favour (“I need a pen”). They must ask three classmates “Can you give me a hand? / Could you lend me…?” and record who said yes.
dynamics.payoff: Requests plus object pronouns, with a written record to correct.

dynamics.name: Who did what to whom?
dynamics.how: Partner A reads six short sentences with names; Partner B repeats each one twice — once with pronouns, once as a question (“Who does she call?”).
dynamics.payoff: Turns statements into questions, the hardest step at A1.

writing.title: A polite invitation
writing.brief: Write a short message inviting somebody to do something with you. Make two offers with “Would you like…?”, ask one question, and use at least three object pronouns.
criteria: “Would you like” + noun, or + to + verb — never both.
Object pronouns after verbs and prepositions.
One question with correct do/does word order.

homework.title: Three polite requests
homework.task: Write three things you need this week and the polite request you would use for each (Can you…? / Could you…? / Would you like…?). Say who you would ask and why that form is polite enough.

test.explain: After the verb “know” we need the object pronoun “her”.
Offers use “Would you like…?”
“Would like” is followed by to + verb.
After the preposition “with” we use the object pronoun “us”.

test.q: Who ___ she invite to the party?
test.explain: “She” takes “does”, and “invite” stays in the base form.

units.title: RIGHT NOW, AT HOME
units.theme: Actions in progress and the people in your family

overview.intro: This unit takes you inside the house at this exact moment: who is cooking, who is studying, who is sleeping. You will use the present continuous for actions happening now, together with the vocabulary of family members, and learn to say how many people do something.
goals: Make questions and answers in the present continuous.
Name family members precisely, including in-laws and cousins.
Use quantifiers to say how many people or things you mean.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe a photo of your family, saying who each person is and what they are doing.

vocab.def: your mother and your father together.
vocab.use: Always plural for the pair. One of them is “my mother” or “my father”, not “my parent”.
examples: My parents live in Medellín.
Do your parents work?
vocab.colloc: my parents · both parents · strict parents

vocab.def: the child of your uncle or aunt.
vocab.use: The same word for a man and a woman — the context tells you which.
examples: My cousin Andrés is a teacher.
I have six cousins on my mother’s side.
vocab.colloc: a close cousin · my favourite cousin

vocab.def: the parents of your parents.
vocab.use: Singular forms: grandmother, grandfather. Informal: grandma, grandpa.
examples: My grandparents live next to us.
I visit my grandmother every Sunday.
vocab.colloc: my grandparents · both grandparents

vocab.def: a person with no brothers or sisters.
vocab.use: Fixed phrase with “an”: “I’m an only child.” Not “only son” unless you mean the only boy.
examples: She is an only child.
I’m not an only child — I have two sisters.
vocab.colloc: an only child · the only child in the family

vocab.def: to take care of someone or something.
vocab.use: Always with “after”: “look after the baby”. Never “look the baby”.
examples: My aunt is looking after my little brother today.
Who looks after the dog when you travel?
vocab.colloc: look after a child · look after the house

vocab.def: right now, at this exact time.
vocab.use: The classic partner of the present continuous. It goes at the start or the end.
examples: At the moment my mother is cooking.
I’m studying English at the moment.
vocab.colloc: at the moment · right now · just now

vocab.def: to become husband and wife.
vocab.use: “Get married” is the event, “be married” is the state: “They got married in May and they are married now.”
examples: My sister is getting married next year.
When did they get married?
vocab.colloc: get married in church · newly married

vocab.def: the sister or brother of your parent, or their partner.
vocab.use: Their children are your cousins. Careful with the pronunciation of “aunt” — it has no “o” sound.
examples: My aunt lives in Bogotá.
I’m staying with my uncle this week.
vocab.colloc: my favourite aunt · a rich uncle

vocab.def: almost the whole group, but not one hundred per cent.
vocab.use: Followed by a plural noun with “the” or a possessive: “nearly all my friends”, “nearly all of them”.
examples: Nearly all my cousins live abroad.
Nearly all of the students passed.
vocab.colloc: nearly all of them · nearly all the time

vocab.def: not a single person.
vocab.use: They are already negative, so the verb stays positive: “No one knows”, never “No one doesn’t know”. Both take a singular verb.
examples: No one is at home right now.
Nobody in my family speaks French.
vocab.colloc: no one else · nobody knows · almost nobody

grammar.name: Present continuous: yes/no and wh-questions
grammar.short: What are you doing? — I’m cooking.
grammar.rule: For an action happening now we use “to be” + verb + -ing. In questions, the form of “to be” moves in front of the subject.
form: Statement: I am working. She is studying. They are eating.
Yes/no: Are you working? Is she studying?
Wh-: What are you doing? Where is he going? Why are they laughing?
notes: Spelling: drop a final -e (make → making); double the consonant after one short vowel (sit → sitting); -ie becomes -y (lie → lying).
Present simple = a habit; present continuous = now: “I work at a bank” vs “I’m working today”.
Some verbs are almost never continuous: like, want, know, need, have (for possession).
examples: What are you doing? — I’m looking after my cousin.
Is your father working today? — No, he isn’t.
They aren’t sleeping; they’re watching a film.
grammar.watch: Do not forget “to be”: “I studying” is wrong — say “I am studying”.
grammar.deep: The present continuous describes what is happening around the moment of speaking, and its shape never changes: a form of “be” plus a verb in -ing. Because “be” is already there, questions need no helper — you simply invert it, exactly as you did in unit 1: “Is she working?” The contrast with the present simple is the point of the tense. “She works in a bank” is a permanent fact; “She is working from home this week” is a temporary situation with an end in sight. That is also why a small group of verbs — know, want, like, need, have (possess), believe — resist the continuous: they describe states, not activities in progress, so “I am knowing her” has nothing to be in progress.

chart.title: Present continuous: form and use
rows: I am cooking. She is studying.
I’m staying with my aunt this week.
I know her. (not I am knowing)

more: What are you doing? — I’m cooking lunch.
Is your father working today? — No, he isn’t.
They aren’t sleeping; they’re watching a film.
Why is the baby crying?
We’re studying for the exam this week.
She’s not answering her phone.

fix.why: The present continuous needs “to be” as well as -ing.
In questions, “are” goes before the subject.
After “to be” the verb takes -ing.

drill.name: Now or every day?
drill.prompt: Say each sentence twice: once as a routine, once as “right now”.
items: I work at home. → I’m working at home right now.

dialogue.line: Hi! What are you doing?
I’m looking after my nephew. He’s playing in the garden.
Is your sister working today?
Yes, she is. She finishes at six.

grammar.sound: The -ing ending is /ɪŋ/, not /in/: say “study-ing” with the sound at the back of the mouth, and do not add a “g” you can hear separately.

grammar.name: Quantifiers: a lot of, nearly all, all, many, not many, few, no one
grammar.short: How many people? Say it without numbers.
grammar.rule: Quantifiers tell us how many, from everybody to nobody. With people and countable nouns the scale runs: all → nearly all → a lot of / many → some → not many / few → no one.
form: all / nearly all + plural noun: All my cousins live here.
a lot of / many + plural noun: A lot of people work at home.
not many / few + plural noun: Few students arrive late. · no one + singular verb: No one is at home.
notes: “No one” takes a singular verb: “No one knows”, not “No one know”.
“Many” is most natural in questions and negatives; “a lot of” is best in positive sentences.
Do not put “of” after “many” unless a determiner follows: “many students”, but “many of my students”.
examples: A lot of my relatives live in the same street.
Nearly all my cousins are older than me.
No one is cooking tonight — we’re ordering food.
grammar.watch: “All” goes before “the/my”: “all my friends”, never “the all my friends”.
grammar.deep: Quantifiers answer the question “how many of them?” without giving a number, and English arranges them on a scale that runs from everybody down to nobody. The two things that decide which one you can use are the type of noun and the shape of the sentence. Plural countable nouns take many, a few, few and “a lot of”; singular uncountable nouns take much and a little, which you will meet properly in unit 8. And “many” behaves differently in questions and negatives than in positive statements: “Do you have many friends?” is completely natural, while “I have many friends” sounds bookish next to “I have a lot of friends”. Remember too that the negative quantifiers — no one, nobody, none — carry the negative by themselves, so the verb after them stays positive.

Use the present continuous with “now”, “today”, “at the moment”.
“No one”, “nobody” and “everybody” are singular in English.

At least three different quantifiers.

Present continuous negatives use “be” + not.

“No one” is the fixed form, with a singular verb.

units.title: HOW OFTEN, HOW GOOD
units.theme: Frequency, free time and asking with “how”

overview.intro: This unit is about how often you do things and how well you do them. You will place adverbs of frequency in the right position and ask precise questions with “how” — how often, how long, how well.
goals: Use adverbs of frequency in the correct place in a sentence.
Ask questions with how often, how long and how well.
Talk about free time, sport and hobbies with short answers.
overview.outcome: By the end you can interview a partner about their hobbies and report how often and how well they do each one.

vocab.def: an activity you enjoy in your free time.
vocab.use: Plural: hobbies. We say “My hobby is painting” or “I like painting”.
examples: My favourite hobby is playing the guitar.
What are your hobbies?
vocab.colloc: a favourite hobby · an expensive hobby

vocab.def: one time / two times.
vocab.use: Frequency: “once a week”, “twice a month”. After two we say “three times a week”.
examples: I go to the gym twice a week.
We meet once a month.
vocab.colloc: once a day · twice a year · three times a week

vocab.def: to do an activity regularly to get better at it.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing: “practise English”, “practise speaking”.
examples: I practise English every evening.
She practises playing the piano for an hour.
vocab.colloc: practise a sport · practise English · practise every day

vocab.def: almost never.
vocab.use: It is already negative, so the verb stays positive: “I hardly ever watch TV.”
examples: He hardly ever eats meat.
I hardly ever go out on Mondays.
vocab.colloc: hardly ever · hardly ever go · almost never

vocab.def: able to do something well.
vocab.use: Always “at”, and the verb after it takes -ing: “good at swimming”.
examples: She is very good at maths.
I’m not good at cooking.
vocab.colloc: good at sport · really good at · not very good at

vocab.def: the hours when you are not working or studying.
vocab.use: No plural: “free time”, never “free times”.
examples: I don’t have much free time this week.
What do you do in your free time?
vocab.colloc: in my free time · a lot of free time

vocab.def: asking about frequency.
vocab.use: Answered with a frequency adverb or a phrase: “once a week”, “every day”, “hardly ever”.
examples: How often do you go to the gym?
How often does the bus come?
vocab.colloc: how often do you · not very often · quite often

vocab.def: “good” describes a person; “well” describes how they do something.
vocab.use: “She is a good singer” but “She sings well”. Never “She sings good”.
examples: He plays the guitar very well.
I’m not very good at swimming.
vocab.colloc: do well · very well · not well at all

vocab.def: nearly every time.
vocab.use: Sits in the same place as “always”: before the main verb, after “to be”.
examples: I almost always walk to work.
She is almost always the first to arrive.
vocab.colloc: almost always late · almost never

vocab.def: to use time or money on something.
vocab.use: “Spend + time + -ing”: “I spend two hours studying.” Never followed by an infinitive.
examples: I spend an hour a day reading.
How much time do you spend online?
vocab.colloc: spend time with · spend money on · spend the weekend

vocab.def: in the hours when you are not working or studying.
vocab.use: Fixed phrase; usually at the start or end. Not “in my frees” or “in free time”.
examples: In my free time I play football.
I read a lot in my free time.
vocab.colloc: in my free time · a lot of free time

vocab.def: to be very interested in something.
vocab.use: Always with “into” + noun or -ing: “I’m into cycling.” Informal.
examples: My brother is really into video games.
I’m not into horror films.
vocab.colloc: be really into · not be into something

grammar.name: Adverbs of frequency
grammar.short: always, almost always, usually, hardly ever, never.
grammar.rule: Adverbs of frequency say how often. The scale is: always → almost always → usually → often → sometimes → hardly ever → never. Their position is fixed: before the main verb, but after “to be”.
form: Before the main verb: I always study at night. She never eats fish.
After “to be”: He is usually late. They are never at home.
Between helper and verb: I have never been to Cali. Do you usually work here?
notes: “Never” and “hardly ever” already make the sentence negative — do not add “don’t”: “I never go”, not “I don’t never go”.
“Sometimes” and “usually” can also start the sentence: “Sometimes I walk to work.”
“Always” cannot start the sentence in a statement.
examples: I usually get up at six.
My brother is always hungry.
She hardly ever answers her phone.
grammar.watch: Position matters more than the word: “I always am tired” is wrong — say “I am always tired”.
grammar.deep: Adverbs of frequency tell your listener how regular a habit is, and English is unusually strict about where they stand. The rule has two halves: they go before the main verb, but after the verb “to be”. So “I always arrive early” and “I am always early” are both correct, and swapping the positions breaks both. With an auxiliary the adverb slips into the middle: “I have never been there”, “I don’t usually work Saturdays”. Two of these words are already negative — never and hardly ever — so the verb after them stays positive: “I hardly ever eat meat”, not “I don’t hardly ever eat meat”. Longer frequency phrases such as “once a week” or “every morning” behave differently: they prefer the end of the sentence, or occasionally the beginning for emphasis.

chart.title: Frequency and position
rows: before main verb, or start of sentence

more: I usually get up at six.
My brother is always hungry.
She hardly ever answers her phone.
We sometimes study together at the weekend.
He is never late for class.
I have never been to Cartagena.

fix.why: With “to be” the adverb goes after the verb.
The -s stays on the main verb even with an adverb in front.
Frequency adverbs go inside the sentence, not at the front.

drill.name: Slide the adverb
drill.prompt: Put the adverb in the right place and say the sentence.
items: They / go to the cinema (hardly ever)
We / are at home on Sundays (usually)

dialogue.line: Do you often go out during the week?
Hardly ever. I’m usually too tired.
And at the weekend?
I almost always see my friends on Saturday.

grammar.sound: “Usually” has three beats in careful speech but two in fast speech: /ˈjuːʒəli/. Don’t say “u-su-al-ly”.

grammar.name: Questions with “how” and short answers
grammar.short: How often? How long? How well?
grammar.rule: “How” plus another word makes a precise question. Each combination asks about a different measurement, and each has its own natural short answer.
form: How often…? → Twice a week. / Every day. / Hardly ever.
How long…? → For two years. / About an hour.
How well / How good at…? → Quite well. / Not very good. / Really well.
notes: “How often” asks about frequency; “how long” asks about duration.
“Good” is an adjective (with “be”), “well” is an adverb (with other verbs): “She is good at singing” / “She sings well”.
Short answers do not repeat the whole sentence: “How often do you swim?” — “Twice a week.”
examples: How often do you play football? — About twice a week.
How long do you practise every day? — For half an hour.
How well does she speak English? — Very well.
grammar.watch: Do not say “How much times?” — the question is “How many times?” or better “How often?”.
grammar.deep: “How” is the most productive question word in English because it combines with other words to measure almost anything. On its own it asks about manner or health (“How are you?”, “How do you get to work?”). Followed by an adjective or adverb it asks for a measurement: how long for duration, how often for frequency, how far for distance, how well for skill. The structure never changes — how + the measuring word, then the ordinary question order — so once you have the pattern, you can build dozens of questions from it. The one thing to watch is “how long”, which measures both time and physical length, so context does the work: “How long is the film?” asks about minutes, “How long is the table?” asks about metres.

rows: How do you get to work?
How well do you speak English?

How long have you studied English? — For two years.
How well do you speak French? — Not very well.
How good are you at maths? — Quite good.
How often does she call you? — Every Sunday.

fix.why: For frequency English uses “How often”, not “how much times”.

fix.wrong: How long time do you study?
fix.why: “How long” already contains the idea of time.
With a verb we need the adverb “well”, not the adjective “good”.

drill.name: Ask with how
drill.prompt: Make the question and give a short answer.

dialogue.line: How often do you play football?
About twice a week.
How well do you play?
Not very well, but I really enjoy it.

grammar.sound: Short answers keep only the important words: “Twice a week”, “For two years” — no need for a full sentence.

Two truths and a lie about your free time, using frequency adverbs. The class finds the lie.

tips: Frequency adverbs: before the verb, after “be”.
“Never” is already negative — one negative per sentence.
Use “How often…?” instead of “How many times…?” whenever you can.

dynamics.payoff: Adverb position gets said out loud by everyone, with the meaning visible.

dynamics.how: Grid of activities. Students ask “How often do you…?” and can only write a name when the answer matches the square (“hardly ever”, “every day”…).
dynamics.payoff: Question form plus the frequency vocabulary, thirty times over.

dynamics.name: Guess my routine
dynamics.how: Partner A writes five secret frequencies about themselves. Partner B guesses each one with a full question; three guesses per item.
dynamics.payoff: Repetition of “Do you usually…?” with a reason to keep asking.

dynamics.payoff: Introduces “how well / how long” without a worksheet.

writing.brief: Write about your week using five different frequency adverbs, then ask three “how” questions you would like a classmate to answer.
criteria: Adverbs are in the correct position, including with “to be”.
Five different adverbs, not the same one twice.
The three questions use different “how” combinations.

homework.title: Track one week
homework.task: For three days, note how often you do one activity (study, exercise, speak English). Write four sentences with different frequency adverbs and one “How often…?” question for your teacher.

test.explain: Once a month is “hardly ever”, not “never”.
With a verb we use the adverb: “How well do you speak…?”

units.title: YESTERDAY’S STORY
units.theme: Talking about finished events in the past

overview.intro: This unit moves you into the past. You will tell what you did with ordinary verbs and the helper “did”, and describe how things were with “was” and “were”. These two patterns cover almost every story you will tell at A1.
goals: Form positive, negative and question sentences in the past simple with “did”.
Use was and were correctly for descriptions and states in the past.
Tell a short story about yesterday or last weekend.
overview.outcome: By the end you can tell a two-minute story about a past day, with at least six past verbs and no missing “did”.

vocab.def: the day before today.
vocab.use: A signal for the past simple. Usually at the end: “I studied yesterday.”
examples: I went to the cinema yesterday.
Yesterday was a long day.
vocab.colloc: yesterday morning · yesterday evening · the day before yesterday

vocab.def: the one before this one (week, month, year).
vocab.use: No “the” and no preposition: “last Monday”, not “in the last Monday”.
examples: Last weekend I visited my grandmother.
We travelled to the coast last year.
vocab.colloc: last night · last week · last summer

vocab.def: before now, counting back from today.
vocab.use: It goes after the period of time: “two days ago”, never “ago two days”.
examples: I finished school three years ago.
They arrived ten minutes ago.
vocab.colloc: a long time ago · a week ago · not long ago

vocab.def: to take place, to occur.
vocab.use: Things happen; people do not happen: “What happened?” Not “What did it happen?”.
examples: What happened at the party?
Something strange happened yesterday.
vocab.colloc: what happened · happen suddenly · happen again

vocab.def: words that put your story in order.
vocab.use: Use them at the start of a sentence to move the story forward.
examples: We had dinner. Then we watched a film.
First I called her. After that, I went home.
vocab.colloc: first · then · after that · finally

vocab.def: to remain in a place, or to sleep somewhere temporarily.
vocab.use: Regular verb: stayed. “Stay at home”, “stay in a hotel”, “stay with a friend”.
examples: I stayed at home all weekend.
We stayed in a small hotel near the beach.
vocab.colloc: stay at home · stay with family · stay for two days

vocab.def: to reach a place.
vocab.use: “Arrive in” a city or country, “arrive at” a building or a point. Never “arrive to”.
examples: We arrived in Bogotá at midnight.
She arrived at the office late.
vocab.colloc: arrive early · arrive on time · arrive at the airport

vocab.def: to get something by paying for it.
vocab.use: Irregular: buy – bought – bought. “Buy something for someone”: “I bought a gift for my mother.”
examples: I bought these shoes last week.
Where did you buy that jacket?
vocab.colloc: buy a ticket · buy online · buy something for someone

vocab.def: to go from one place to another, usually far.
vocab.use: “Travel to + place”, and “travel by + transport”: “travel by bus”. The noun for one journey is “a trip”.
examples: Last year we travelled to Peru.
I travel by train every Monday.
vocab.colloc: travel abroad · travel by plane · travel light

vocab.def: not interesting / holding your attention.
vocab.use: They describe the thing, not the person: “The film was boring” and “I was bored”.
examples: The class was interesting yesterday.
It was a boring weekend.
vocab.colloc: really boring · very interesting · sounds interesting

vocab.def: two days ago.
vocab.use: A fixed phrase; the shorter “two days ago” is more common in speech.
examples: I saw her the day before yesterday.
We arrived the day before yesterday.
vocab.colloc: the day before yesterday · two days ago

vocab.def: to enjoy yourself a lot.
vocab.use: Past: “We had a great time.” Never “I passed a great time”.
examples: We had a great time at the party.
Did you have a good time in Cali?
vocab.colloc: have a great / good / terrible time

grammar.name: Past simple with ordinary verbs (did)
grammar.short: I worked. Did you work? I didn’t work.
grammar.rule: For finished actions in the past, regular verbs add -ed and many common verbs are irregular. In questions and negatives we use the helper “did” and the verb returns to its base form.
form: Positive: I worked / she studied / we went / he had.
Negative: I didn’t work. She didn’t go.
Question: Did you work yesterday? What did she say?
notes: Spelling: -e → -ed (live → lived); consonant + y → -ied (study → studied); double the consonant (stop → stopped).
After “did” or “didn’t”, never use the past form: “Did you go?”, not “Did you went?”.
Irregular verbs to learn first: go → went, have → had, do → did, see → saw, say → said, get → got, make → made.
examples: I studied English for two hours yesterday.
Did you see the film last night?
She didn’t come to class on Monday.
grammar.watch: One past marker per sentence — either on “did” or on the verb, never on both.
grammar.deep: The past simple takes a finished action and presents it as one closed block of time, which is why it lives so naturally with markers such as yesterday, last week and two years ago. Regular verbs add -ed, and irregular ones change shape completely, so the only shortcut is to learn them in threes and in sound families: buy–bought–bought sits beside bring–brought–brought, and think–thought–thought sounds the same. The grammar itself is simpler than the vocabulary. Once “did” appears in a negative or a question, the past is already marked, so the main verb returns to its base form: “Did you go?”, “I didn’t go.” Learners who write “Did you went?” have marked the past twice, and that doubled marking is the single most common A1 past-tense error.

drill.prompt: Say each sentence positive, negative and as a question.

grammar.name: Past simple of “to be” (was / were)
grammar.short: I was, you were, it was, they were.
grammar.rule: “To be” does not use “did”. It has its own two past forms: “was” for I, he, she, it, and “were” for you, we, they. Questions invert; negatives add “not”.
form: Positive: I was tired. They were at home.
Negative: I wasn’t tired. They weren’t at home.
Question: Was it good? Where were you? Short answers: Yes, I was. / No, they weren’t.
notes: “There was” for one thing, “there were” for several: “There was a party”, “There were many people”.
Use was/were for states and descriptions; use “did” verbs for actions.
Never mix them: “I was went” is wrong.
examples: The film was really good.
We were at my aunt’s house all afternoon.
Where were you yesterday? — I was at work.
grammar.watch: Do not add “did” to “to be”: “Did you were there?” is wrong — say “Were you there?”.
grammar.deep: “To be” keeps its own past, and it keeps its own grammar with it. Where ordinary verbs need the helper “did”, was and were form negatives and questions on their own: “I wasn’t ready”, “Were you there?”. That independence is why mixing the two systems produces the classic error “Did you were at home?” — two helpers competing for one job. Choose the system before you start the sentence: if the sentence has an action, you need did plus a base verb; if it only links a subject to a description, a place or an age, you need was or were. Notice also that English uses “to be” where several other languages use “to have”: age (“I was twenty”), hunger and cold (“I was cold”) and correctness (“You were right”) all take was or were.

They were at home all day.
It wasn’t expensive.
We weren’t ready.
Was the food good? — Yes, it was.
Where were you yesterday?

“They” takes “were”.
“You” always takes “were”.

I was at the doctor’s. It was a long morning.

Yes, it was fine, thanks.

grammar.sound: In fast speech “was” and “were” are unstressed: /wəz/, /wə/. Stress them only to correct somebody: “I WAS there!”

“Was/were” never take “did”.

quiz.explain: “Go” is an ordinary verb, so the past question uses the helper “did” + base form.

dynamics.name: Yesterday chain
dynamics.how: Each student adds one past-simple sentence to build a class story about yesterday. Any “didn’t went” style error sends the sentence back for repair by the same student.
dynamics.payoff: Immediate public correction of the two classic past errors.

dynamics.how: Two students invent where they were last night. The class questions them separately with past questions; the pair loses if three answers contradict.

dynamics.name: Photo memory
dynamics.how: Each student shows an old photo and gives three past sentences. The group asks two questions each, one with “did” and one with “was/were”.
dynamics.payoff: Separates the two past systems inside one topic.

dynamics.name: Verb sort
dynamics.how: Give 24 verb cards. Groups sort them into regular and irregular, then read the past form aloud and check the -ed sound (/t/, /d/, /ɪd/).
dynamics.payoff: Fixes the pronunciation problem before it becomes a habit.

writing.title: One day I remember
writing.brief: Write about one day in the past: where you were, what you did, who you were with, and one thing that did not happen. Use both “did” verbs and “was/were”.
criteria: No sentence has two past markers.
“Was / were” used with the right subjects.
At least two irregular past verbs.

homework.title: Message a friend about yesterday

units.title: MY TOWN, MY PLACE

overview.intro: This unit puts things on the map. You will say what exists in a place with “there is” and “there are”, put objects in position with prepositions of place, and ask about quantity with “how much” and “how many”.
goals: Use there is / there are correctly in statements, negatives and questions.
Describe exact positions with prepositions of place.
Ask about quantity with how much and how many and answer with quantifiers.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe your neighbourhood or your room in detail so that a partner can draw it.

vocab.def: the small area of a city where you live.
vocab.use: Use “in”: “in my neighbourhood”. US spelling: neighborhood.
examples: There are two parks in my neighbourhood.
It’s a quiet neighbourhood.
vocab.colloc: a quiet neighbourhood · a safe neighbourhood

vocab.def: the point where two streets or two walls meet.
vocab.use: “On the corner” for streets, “in the corner” for a room.
examples: There is a pharmacy on the corner.
The lamp is in the corner of the room.
vocab.colloc: on the corner · around the corner · in the corner

vocab.def: in the middle of two things.
vocab.use: Two things only, joined by “and”: “between the bank and the shop”.
examples: My house is between the school and the park.
Sit between us.
vocab.colloc: between A and B · right between

vocab.def: on the other side of the street, facing it.
vocab.use: US English; UK English prefers “opposite”. Both are followed directly by the noun.
examples: The bakery is across from the bank.
There is a bus stop across from my building.
vocab.colloc: across from the park · directly across from

vocab.def: full of people / with few people and little noise.
vocab.use: Both describe places: “a crowded market”, “a quiet street”.
examples: The centre is crowded at six o’clock.
My street is very quiet at night.
vocab.colloc: a crowded street · a quiet area

vocab.def: a small number / a small amount.
vocab.use: “A few” with countable nouns (a few shops); “a little” with uncountable nouns (a little water).
examples: There are a few restaurants near here.
I only have a little money.
vocab.colloc: a few people · a little time · a little money

vocab.def: a group of buildings between two streets; also a tall building of flats.
vocab.use: Very useful in directions: “It’s two blocks from here.”
examples: The pharmacy is three blocks away.
I live in a block of flats near the park.
vocab.colloc: two blocks away · a block of flats · around the block

vocab.def: with little sound / with a lot of unwanted sound.
vocab.use: “Quiet” describes places and people; “silent” means no sound at all. The noun is “noise”.
examples: My street is quiet at night.
The bar next door is very noisy.
vocab.colloc: a quiet street · too noisy · keep quiet

vocab.def: the tables, chairs, beds and sofas in a room.
vocab.use: Uncountable: “some furniture”, “a piece of furniture” — never “furnitures” and never “a furniture”.
examples: There isn’t much furniture in my room.
We bought two pieces of furniture.
vocab.colloc: a piece of furniture · old furniture · office furniture

vocab.def: a small amount — “a little” for uncountable, “a few” for countable.
vocab.use: “A little milk” but “a few eggs”. Without “a”, they turn negative: “little time” means not enough.
examples: There’s a little milk in the fridge and a few eggs.
I only need a little help.
vocab.colloc: a little water · a few minutes · very little time

vocab.def: close enough to walk to.
vocab.use: Usually with “be”: “The park is within walking distance.”
examples: Everything is within walking distance of my flat.
The school isn’t within walking distance.
vocab.colloc: within walking distance of · just around the corner

vocab.def: full of people.
vocab.use: For places, not people: “a crowded bus”. The noun is “a crowd”.
examples: The centre is very crowded on Saturdays.
It was too crowded, so we left.
vocab.colloc: a crowded street · get crowded · very crowded

grammar.name: There is / there are + prepositions of place
grammar.short: There is a park next to my house.
grammar.rule: “There is / there are” says that something exists in a place. Use “there is” with a singular or uncountable noun and “there are” with a plural. Prepositions of place then say exactly where.
form: There is a bank. / There isn’t a cinema. / Is there a pharmacy near here?
There are two parks. / There aren’t any shops. / Are there any hotels?
in · on · in front of · behind · next to · between · across from · near.
notes: With a list, the verb agrees with the first noun: “There is a sofa and two chairs.”
Use “any” in negatives and questions: “There aren’t any buses.”
“There” is not a place here — it is a grammar word. The real place goes at the end: “There is a park in my street.”
examples: There is a supermarket next to my building.
There are three cafés across from the park.
Is there a bus stop near here?
grammar.watch: Do not confuse “there is” (exists) with “it is” (identifies): “There is a hotel. It is very old.”
grammar.deep: “There is” and “there are” exist to announce that something is present in a place. The word “there” here is not a place — it is a grammatical placeholder, which is why the sentence still needs a real location at the end: “There is a bank on the corner.” The verb agrees with what comes immediately after it, so a list takes its number from the first item: “There is a table and four chairs.” Around this frame sit the prepositions of place, and they repay careful learning because English keeps them fixed: in for enclosed spaces, on for surfaces, at for points. The longer ones — in front of, next to, behind, across from, between — are learned as whole phrases, and note that “in front of” is the opposite of “behind”, not of “next to”.

There are two schools on this street.

next to, in front of, behind

Is there a bus stop near here?

fix.why: A plural noun needs “there are”.

fix.wrong: It is a park near my house.
fix.right: There is a park near my house.
fix.why: “There is” says something exists; “it is” identifies something already mentioned.

fix.wrong: There are a lot of traffic.
fix.right: There is a lot of traffic.
fix.why: “Traffic” is uncountable, so it takes “there is”.

drill.name: Map it
drill.prompt: Look around the room (or at a map) and say one sentence for each preposition.

dialogue.line: Is there a pharmacy near here?
Yes, there’s one across from the bank.
Are there any cash machines on this street?
There aren’t any here, but there are two in the mall.

contrast.title: there is / there are / it is
rows: There is a lot of noise.

grammar.sound: “There’s” and “there are” sound almost the same in fast speech — the plural noun is what tells the listener which one you said. Say the noun clearly.

grammar.name: How much / how many + quantifiers
grammar.short: How many shops? How much traffic?
grammar.rule: Use “how many” with countable nouns you can count one by one, and “how much” with uncountable nouns you cannot. Answers use quantifiers: a lot, many, much, few, little.
form: How many + plural noun: How many rooms are there?
How much + uncountable noun: How much traffic is there?
Answers: A lot. · Not many. · Only a few. · Not much. · Very little.
notes: Common uncountable nouns: water, money, time, traffic, noise, bread, information.
“Much” is mostly for questions and negatives: “There isn’t much noise.”
“A few” is positive (some), “few” is negative (almost none). The same goes for “a little” and “little”.
examples: How many people live in your building?
How much time do you need?
There aren’t many shops, but there are a few cafés.
grammar.watch: “How many money” is a classic error — money is uncountable, so it is “How much money?”.
grammar.deep: “How much” and “how many” are the same question asked of two different kinds of noun, and choosing between them forces you to decide what kind of noun you have. If you can put a number in front of it, it is countable and takes “how many”: how many eggs, how many people. If you can only measure it, it is uncountable and takes “how much”: how much milk, how much time, how much money. Uncountable nouns also take a singular verb and no plural -s, which is why “informations” and “advices” are never possible. When you do need to count an uncountable noun, English lends you a container or a unit: a bottle of water, two pieces of advice, three slices of bread. That trick is what lets you be precise about anything, countable or not.

more: How many rooms are there in your house?

There aren’t many parks in my area.

There’s very little space in the centre.

fix.why: “Traffic” is uncountable, so we use “how much”.
“Many” goes with countable plurals.
“Few” is for countable nouns, “little” for uncountable.

drill.name: Countable or not?
drill.prompt: Ask the question with how much or how many.
