About forty. But there isn’t much space for cars.
How much noise is there at night?
Very little — it’s a quiet street.

grammar.sound: “How much” and “how many” are said as one unit with the stress on MUCH / MAny.

A tourist asks where the bank, pharmacy and bus stop are. Use prepositions of place in every answer.
Ask three classmates how many shops, parks and schools there are in their neighbourhood. Compare.

tips: Count the noun first: countable → there are / how many; uncountable → there is / how much.
Use “any” after negatives and in questions: “Are there any…?”
“Between” always takes two things joined by “and”.

quiz.explain: “Restaurants” is plural, and it is a question, so we invert: “Are there any…?”

dynamics.name: Blind map
dynamics.how: Partner A has a simple map with eight places; Partner B has an empty grid. A describes with “There is… next to…” until B’s map matches. No pointing, no naming grid squares.
dynamics.payoff: Prepositions of place become the only tool that works.

dynamics.name: Neighbourhood advert
dynamics.how: Groups invent a neighbourhood and sell it to the class in 60 seconds using at least six “there is / there are” sentences. The class votes on where they would live.
dynamics.payoff: Repetition inside a persuasive task.

dynamics.name: How much, how many
dynamics.how: Twelve cards with nouns (traffic, shops, noise, parks…). Students collect cards by asking a correct question about each one to a classmate.
dynamics.payoff: Sorts countable from uncountable through use, not rules.

dynamics.name: Spot the difference
dynamics.how: Two similar street pictures. Students find six differences, each stated as “In my picture there is… but in yours there are…”.
dynamics.payoff: Forces the singular/plural choice in every sentence.

writing.title: My street
writing.brief: Describe your street or neighbourhood: what there is, what there isn’t, and how much traffic and noise there is. Use at least four prepositions of place.
criteria: “There is” and “there are” agree with the noun.
Four different prepositions of place.
“How much / how many” used correctly if you include a question.

homework.task: Draw a simple map of the five places closest to your home. Label them, then write five sentences with “there is / there are” and a preposition of place.

test.explain: “Traffic” is uncountable, so “how much”.
The preposition is “next to”.

test.explain: “Noise” is uncountable, so it takes “there isn’t”.

test.q: There are only ___ shops on my street.
test.explain: “Shops” is countable, so “a few”.

units.title: WHAT DO THEY LOOK LIKE?
units.theme: Describing people’s appearance and identifying them

overview.intro: This unit is about describing people so well that someone can find them in a crowd. You will ask about appearance, use adjectives in the right order, and identify one person among many with participles: “the one wearing a red jacket”.
goals: Ask and answer questions about physical appearance.
Use appearance vocabulary: height, build, hair, eyes, clothes.
Identify a person with a modifier: Which one is she? — The one talking to Ana.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe three people in a photo so precisely that a partner points to the right one every time.

vocab.def: of great height / of little height.
vocab.use: For people we use “tall”, not “high”. Buildings can be high or tall; people are only tall.
examples: My brother is very tall.
She is short with long hair.
vocab.colloc: quite tall · really short · tall and thin

vocab.def: to have clothes on your body.
vocab.use: Very often in the continuous for now: “She is wearing a blue dress.” Irregular past: wore.
examples: He is wearing glasses and a white shirt.
What are you wearing to the party?
vocab.colloc: wear glasses · wear a uniform · wear black

vocab.def: hair with no waves / hair with lots of waves.
vocab.use: They go before “hair”: “long curly hair”. Order: length + style + colour.
examples: She has long curly hair.
My hair is short and straight.
vocab.colloc: straight hair · curly hair · dark curly hair

vocab.def: to have a similar appearance to someone.
vocab.use: “What does she look like?” asks about appearance. “What is she like?” asks about personality. Do not mix them.
examples: What does your father look like?
She looks like her mother.
vocab.colloc: look like someone · look like a student

vocab.def: hair on the chin / hair above the mouth.
vocab.use: We “have” a beard, or we say someone is “with a beard”.
examples: The man with the beard is my uncle.
He has a small moustache.
vocab.colloc: a full beard · have a beard · grow a beard

vocab.def: between about forty and sixty years old.
vocab.use: A polite way to describe age without a number. Before the noun: “a middle-aged woman”.
examples: A middle-aged man asked for directions.
My parents are middle-aged.
vocab.colloc: a middle-aged couple · middle-aged and friendly

vocab.def: what grows on your head.
vocab.use: Uncountable when it is all of it: “She has long hair”, never “hairs”. Colour and length go before it: “short dark hair”.
examples: He has short black hair.
My sister has beautiful curly hair.
vocab.colloc: long hair · dark hair · cut your hair

vocab.def: the part of the face you see with.
vocab.use: With “have”: “She has green eyes.” Never “She is green eyes”.
examples: He has big brown eyes.
Both my parents have blue eyes.
vocab.colloc: brown eyes · dark eyes · beautiful eyes

vocab.def: attractive.
vocab.use: Used for men and women. “Handsome” is mostly for men, “pretty” mostly for women.
examples: Her brother is very good-looking.
He’s a good-looking guy.
vocab.colloc: really good-looking · a good-looking couple

vocab.term: to be like / to look like
vocab.def: “be like” asks about personality; “look like” asks about appearance.
vocab.use: “What is she like?” — She’s kind and funny. “What does she look like?” — She’s tall with dark hair.
examples: What is your new boss like?
What does your brother look like?
vocab.colloc: what’s he like · look like your mother

vocab.def: thin in a good way / with a strong, solid body.
vocab.use: “Slim” is the polite word for thin about people; “skinny” sounds negative. “Well-built” describes a strong body, usually a man’s.
examples: She’s tall and slim.
Her husband is short and well-built.
vocab.colloc: quite slim · very well-built · slim and athletic

vocab.def: to look like or behave like an older relative.
vocab.use: Only for family: “He takes after his father.” Not separable, and not used in the continuous.
examples: I take after my mother — same eyes, same voice.
Who does your daughter take after?
vocab.colloc: take after your mother · really take after him

grammar.name: Wh-questions about descriptions
grammar.short: What do you look like? What is she like?
grammar.rule: To ask about appearance we use “look like”; to ask about personality we use “be like”. Both are questions with normal wh-word order.
form: What + do/does + subject + look like? → What does he look like?
What + be + subject + like? → What is she like?
Answers: He is tall with short dark hair. / She is friendly and very funny.
notes: The answer to “look like” has no “like” in it: “He is tall”, not “He looks like tall”.
Use “have got / have” for features: “She has green eyes.”
Adjective order before a noun: size + age + shape + colour: “a tall young woman with long black hair”.
examples: What does your sister look like? — She is short with curly hair.
What is your new teacher like? — Very patient.
He looks like his father.
grammar.watch: “How does she look?” asks about today only (nice, tired). “What does she look like?” asks about her permanent appearance.
grammar.deep: Descriptions in English divide into two questions that look almost identical and mean completely different things. “What does she look like?” asks about appearance and is answered with height, hair, eyes and clothes. “What is she like?” asks about personality and is answered with adjectives of character. Learners mix them constantly, and the mistake matters, because the answers do not overlap at all. Once you have chosen the question, the answer follows a fixed order: “She is” plus a general description, then “she has” plus body features, then “she is wearing” plus clothes. English also prefers a particular adjective order in front of a noun — size, then age, then colour — so “short dark hair” sounds right and “dark short hair” sounds foreign, even though both are grammatically legal.

chart.title: Two ways of describing a person
rows: He’s tall and he has short hair.

more: What does your best friend look like?
She’s about my height, with long straight hair.
He’s in his thirties and he wears glasses.
My cousin is tall, slim and very quiet.
What are your neighbours like? — Really friendly.
He takes after his father: same nose, same walk.

fix.why: The question word for appearance is “what”, and the helper is “do/does”.
“Look like” is followed by a noun, not an adjective: “She looks like her sister.”

fix.wrong: She has a dark long hair.
fix.why: Adjective order is length before colour, and “hair” takes no article here.

drill.name: Two questions, one person
drill.prompt: For each person, ask both questions and give a two-part answer: appearance first, personality second.

dialogue.line: I’m meeting my cousin at the airport. What does she look like?
She’s quite tall, with short curly hair.
And what is she like? Is she talkative?
Very. She takes after our grandmother.

grammar.sound: In “What does he look like?” the words run together: /wɒdəzi/. Practise the whole question as three beats, not five.

grammar.name: Modifiers with present participles
grammar.short: Which one is she? — The one wearing the red coat.
grammar.rule: To pick one person out of a group we add a participle phrase (verb + -ing) directly after the noun or after “the one”. It works like a short relative clause.
form: The + noun + -ing phrase: the woman standing near the door.
The one / the ones + -ing phrase: The one talking to Ana.
With a preposition instead: the man in the blue jacket, the girl with the glasses.
notes: No “to be” inside the phrase: “the man standing there”, not “the man is standing there”.
“The one” replaces a singular person, “the ones” a plural group.
You can combine both types: “the tall one wearing glasses”.
examples: Which one is your brother? — The one wearing the black cap.
The woman talking to the teacher is my mother.
Do you see the two students sitting at the back?
grammar.watch: Put the -ing phrase straight after the person it describes, or the sentence changes meaning.
grammar.deep: A present participle — the -ing form — can act like an adjective and pick one person out of a group: “the woman wearing the red coat”, “the man standing by the door”. What you are really doing is shortening a relative clause: “the woman who is wearing the red coat” loses “who is”, and the meaning stays identical. This is how English answers the question “Which one?” without a long sentence, and it is why photo descriptions and identifications lean on it so heavily. Two rules keep it safe. The participle must come immediately after the noun it describes, or it attaches to the wrong person. And the participle carries no tense of its own — the main verb does that job, so “the man sitting there was my teacher” is perfectly correct.

drill.prompt: Identify a classmate using only “the one…”. The class guesses. No names, no pointing.

The one writing on the board.
And the man next to her?
That’s the director — the one wearing the blue tie.

the one who is my cousin

Describe a famous person’s appearance. Your partner guesses in five questions or fewer.
You are meeting someone at the airport. Describe on the phone what you look like and what you are wearing.

tips: “What is he like?” = personality. “What does he look like?” = appearance.
Order the hair: length, then style, then colour — “long curly brown hair”.
“The one wearing…” is the quickest way to identify someone.

quiz.q: Which one is your cousin? — The one ___ the red jacket.

writing.brief: Choose a photo with at least three people. Write a paragraph describing each one so a reader could point to them. Give appearance for all three, and personality for the one you know.

Adjective order is correct: size, age, colour.
At least one sentence uses “What is he/she like?” information.

homework.task: Record 60 seconds describing a person your classmate does not know. Then ask a family member to describe you in Spanish and translate their description into English in five written sentences.

test.explain: Appearance questions use “do/does” + “look like”; “your brother” takes “does”.
Length comes before colour: “long dark hair”.

test.explain: After “the one” we use the -ing form with no verb “to be”.
“What is he like?” asks about personality.

test.q: He ___ his father — same eyes, same voice.

units.title: DONE AND NOT DONE YET
units.theme: Talking about experience and completed tasks

overview.intro: This unit gives you the tense English uses for results and experience: the present perfect. You will say what you have already done, what you haven’t done yet, and learn when to switch back to the past simple.
goals: Form the present perfect with have/has + past participle.
Use “already” and “yet” in the right position.
Choose between present perfect and past simple correctly.
overview.outcome: By the end you can go through a to-do list saying what you have already done and what you haven’t done yet.

vocab.def: before now, sooner than expected.
vocab.use: Positive sentences. It goes between “have” and the participle: “I have already eaten.”
examples: I have already finished my homework.
She has already left the office.
vocab.colloc: already done · already finished · already there

vocab.def: up to now (used for things not done).
vocab.use: Only in negatives and questions, and always at the end: “I haven’t called her yet.”
examples: Have you eaten yet?
They haven’t arrived yet.
vocab.colloc: not yet · have you… yet? · not finished yet

vocab.def: at any time in your life / at no time in your life.
vocab.use: “Ever” is for questions: “Have you ever been to Peru?” “Never” is the negative answer.
examples: Have you ever flown in a plane?
I have never eaten sushi.
vocab.colloc: have you ever… · never been · never tried

vocab.def: to reserve a ticket, table or room in advance.
vocab.use: Regular verb: booked. Very common in travel contexts.
examples: I’ve already booked the tickets.
Have you booked a table?
vocab.colloc: book a flight · book a room · book online

vocab.def: to put your things into a bag or suitcase.
vocab.use: Regular verb: packed. “Pack a suitcase”, “pack for a trip”.
examples: I haven’t packed my suitcase yet.
She packed everything last night.
vocab.colloc: pack a bag · pack clothes · finish packing

vocab.def: the things you have done and learnt in life or work.
vocab.use: Uncountable when it means knowledge: “a lot of experience”, not “many experiences” in that sense.
examples: She has a lot of experience with children.
It was a great experience.
vocab.colloc: work experience · a lot of experience · a good experience

vocab.def: a very short time ago.
vocab.use: Goes between “have” and the participle: “I have just finished.” Different from “only”, which means nothing more.
examples: She has just left the office.
I’ve just had lunch.
vocab.colloc: just arrived · just now · I’ve just finished

vocab.def: up to now, in a period that is not over.
vocab.use: A present perfect signal, usually at the end: “I’ve read two chapters so far.”
examples: So far, everything is fine.
How many have you sold so far?
vocab.colloc: so far so good · so far this year

vocab.def: “since” gives a starting point; “for” gives a length of time.
vocab.use: Since 2020, since Monday · for three years, for a long time. Both go with the present perfect.
examples: I’ve lived here since 2019.
I’ve lived here for seven years.
vocab.colloc: ever since · for ages · since last week

vocab.def: to bring something to its end.
vocab.use: “Finish” takes a noun or -ing (“finish eating”); “complete” is more formal and takes a noun (“complete the form”).
examples: Have you finished the exercise yet?
I completed the course last month.
vocab.colloc: finish early · finish the report · complete a form

vocab.def: to have no more of something.
vocab.use: Always with “of” before the thing: “We’ve run out of milk.” Very common in the present perfect.
examples: We’ve run out of coffee.
I ran out of time before the last question.
vocab.colloc: run out of money · run out of time · run out of ideas

grammar.name: Present perfect with “already” and “yet”
grammar.short: I’ve already done it. I haven’t done it yet.
grammar.rule: The present perfect is have/has + past participle. It links the past with now: the action is finished, but the result matters at this moment. “Already” marks what is done; “yet” marks what is still missing.
form: Positive: I have (’ve) already eaten. She has (’s) already left.
Negative: I haven’t finished yet. He hasn’t called yet.
Question: Have you eaten yet? Has she arrived yet?
notes: Past participles: regular = -ed (finished); irregular = third form (go → gone, see → seen, do → done, be → been).
“Already” sits between the helper and the participle; “yet” goes at the very end.
Use “has” only with he, she and it; use “have” with everyone else.
examples: I’ve already booked the hotel.
We haven’t packed our bags yet.
Has your brother finished university yet?
grammar.watch: Do not use “yet” in positive sentences — the positive word is “already”.
grammar.deep: The present perfect connects the past to now, and “already” and “yet” are the two words that tell your listener whether the connection is good news or bad. “Already” means sooner than expected and belongs in positive sentences, usually between “have” and the participle: “I’ve already sent it.” “Yet” means the thing is still missing, and it belongs at the very end of negatives and questions: “I haven’t sent it yet”, “Have you sent it yet?”. The two are almost mirror images, and swapping them produces sentences English speakers cannot parse. Note that “already” can appear in a question, but then it changes the meaning to surprise: “Have you already finished?” means you did it faster than I thought possible.

chart.title: Already, yet, just, still
rows: Have you ever been to Peru?

more: I’ve already sent the email.
She hasn’t called me yet.
Have you finished the report yet?
They’ve already booked the tickets.
We haven’t decided yet.
He’s already left — you’ve just missed him.

fix.why: “Yet” belongs to negatives and questions; the positive word is “already”.
In a negative, “yet” goes at the very end of the sentence.
The present perfect needs the past participle, not the past simple.

drill.name: The checklist
drill.prompt: Look at a to-do list with five items, three ticked. Say each one with “already” or “yet”.

dialogue.line: Are you ready for tomorrow?
Almost. I’ve already packed and I’ve printed the tickets.
Have you called the hotel yet?
No, not yet. And I haven’t changed any money.

contrast.title: already · yet · just · still
rows: Have you ever paid by card?

grammar.sound: “Have you” becomes /həvjə/ and “haven’t” keeps a clear /n̩t/. Practise: “Have you finished yet?” in three beats.

grammar.name: Present perfect vs past simple
grammar.short: When you say WHEN, use the past simple.
grammar.rule: Use the present perfect when the time is not important or not finished. Use the past simple as soon as you say exactly when it happened.
form: Present perfect: I have been to Cartagena. (some time in my life)
Past simple: I went to Cartagena in 2019. (finished time)
Typical partners: ever, never, already, yet, so far → perfect. Yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago → past simple.
notes: Conversations often begin in the perfect and continue in the past: “Have you seen it?” — “Yes, I saw it on Friday.”
Never combine the perfect with a finished time: “I have gone yesterday” is wrong.
“Been” means you went and came back; “gone” means you are still away.
examples: Have you ever visited Peru? — Yes, I went there two years ago.
She has finished the report. She finished it this morning.
I haven’t seen that film yet.
grammar.watch: The moment a past time word appears (yesterday, last night, in July), switch to the past simple.
grammar.deep: Both tenses talk about the past, but they frame time differently, and the time expression in the sentence almost always decides for you. The past simple needs a finished period — yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago — a box that nothing more can be added to. The present perfect needs an open period — today, this week, in my life so far — or no time at all, when only the present result matters. That is why “I have seen him yesterday” is impossible: a closed box cannot host an open tense. In practice the two work as a team. English opens with the perfect to ask about experience and then switches to the past for the details: “Have you been to Cartagena?” — “Yes, I went two years ago.” Learning that two-step is worth more than any list of rules.

chart.title: Which past tense?
rows: I lived in Cali when I was a child.
Have you ever flown at night?
She’s worked here for six years.
no time given, result matters now

more: I’ve been to Cartagena twice.
I went there in 2019 with my sister.
Have you ever tried ajiaco? — Yes, I tried it last month.
She’s worked here since March.
He worked in Cali for two years, then he moved.
We haven’t seen that film yet, but we saw the first one.

fix.why: A finished time expression forces the past simple.
Something that started in the past and continues takes the present perfect.

fix.wrong: Did you ever go to Peru?
fix.right: Have you ever been to Peru?
fix.why: “Ever” asking about a whole life takes the present perfect.

drill.name: Perfect then past
drill.prompt: Ask with the present perfect; answer with the past simple and one detail.

dialogue.line: Have you ever been to the coast?
Yes, I have. I went to Santa Marta two years ago.
Did you like it?
I loved it. I’ve wanted to go back ever since.

contrast.title: Which past?
rows: I’ve had it for a year.

grammar.sound: Contract “have” in speech: “I’ve been”, “she’s gone”, “we’ve finished”. The full form only appears in short answers.

speaking.text: Make a five-item to-do list for a trip. Tell your partner what you have already done and what you haven’t done yet.
“Have you ever…?” Ask five classmates about unusual experiences. Follow up with “When did you…?”
A boss checks the tasks with an employee before a meeting. Use already and yet in every answer.

tips: Present perfect = no exact time. Past simple = exact time.
“Yet” lives at the end of negatives and questions only.
Learn the third form of the top twenty irregular verbs — you need it here.

quiz.explain: In negative sentences we use “yet” at the end.

dynamics.name: Find someone who has…
dynamics.how: Grid of nine experiences (“has broken a bone”, “has eaten insects”). Students ask “Have you ever…?” and, when the answer is yes, one follow-up in the past simple before writing the name.
dynamics.payoff: Drills the perfect-then-past switch, which is the real skill of this unit.

dynamics.name: The unfinished flat
dynamics.how: Give a picture of a half-decorated room and a list of eight jobs. In pairs, students say which are already done and which haven’t been done yet, then agree on the next three.
dynamics.payoff: Every sentence needs already or yet, with visual evidence to argue about.

dynamics.name: Liar’s CV
dynamics.how: Each student writes four experiences with the present perfect; one is invented. The group interrogates with past-simple questions (“When did you go? Who with?”) and votes.
dynamics.payoff: The interrogation forces the tense switch naturally, and the lie usually collapses in the past simple.

dynamics.name: So far this week
dynamics.how: Each student adds one true sentence with “so far this week I’ve…”. No repetition allowed; a repeat sends you out of the circle.
dynamics.payoff: Quick, personal, and fixes “so far” as a present-perfect signal.

writing.title: Two weeks before the trip
writing.brief: You are organising a trip. Write a short message to the person travelling with you: what you have already done, what you haven’t done yet, and what you did last week that they should know about.
criteria: At least two sentences with “already” and two with “yet”.
At least one past-simple sentence with a finished time expression.
All participles correct: been, done, bought, sent, made.

homework.title: Experience list plus proof
homework.task: Write eight “I have never…” sentences that are true for you. For three of them, add a past-simple sentence explaining the closest you have come. Bring the list ready to read aloud.

test.explain: In a negative, “yet” goes at the end.
“Last Friday” is a finished time, so the past simple is required.
“Ever” about your whole life takes the present perfect.
“Since” gives a starting point; “for” gives a length of time.

test.q: They’ve ___ eaten, so they aren’t hungry.
test.explain: “Already” goes between “have” and the participle in a positive sentence.

Left: did / didn’t + base. Right: have / has + participle.
A word strip: already · yet · just · ever · never · still · so far.
A boxed model pair: “Have you been to Cali?” / “Yes, I went in 2019.”
Corner error: “I have seen him yesterday.”

units.title: REALLY GOOD ADVICE
units.theme: Making descriptions stronger and giving recommendations

overview.intro: This unit gives your English more colour and more usefulness: adverbs to make adjectives stronger or softer, conjunctions to join your ideas, and the modals “can” and “should” to recommend things to other people.
goals: Use adverbs like very, really and quite before adjectives.
Join ideas with and, but, so and because.
Give recommendations with can and should.
overview.outcome: By the end you can recommend three places in your city, with reasons, in connected sentences.

vocab.def: very, to a high degree.
vocab.use: Before an adjective or a verb: “really nice”, “I really like it”. More natural than “very” in speech.
examples: The food is really good here.
I really enjoyed the trip.
vocab.colloc: really good · really important · really like

vocab.def: fairly, a medium amount.
vocab.use: Weaker than “very”: “quite good” is good, but not excellent.
examples: The hotel is quite cheap.
It was quite a long journey.
vocab.colloc: quite good · quite expensive · quite far

vocab.def: to say that something is good and that someone should try it.
vocab.use: Patterns: recommend + noun, or recommend + -ing. Not “recommend to do”.
examples: I recommend the fish — it’s excellent.
She recommended visiting the old town.
vocab.colloc: highly recommend · recommend a restaurant

vocab.def: good enough for the money, time or effort.
vocab.use: Fixed phrase: “It’s worth it.” For actions: “It’s worth visiting.”
examples: The museum costs more, but it’s worth it.
It’s worth going early.
vocab.colloc: well worth it · not worth it · worth visiting

vocab.def: the word that introduces a result.
vocab.use: “It was late, so we went home.” Cause first, result after “so”.
examples: It was raining, so we stayed inside.
The bus was full, so I walked.
vocab.colloc: so I · so we decided

vocab.def: the word that introduces a reason.
vocab.use: “We stayed inside because it was raining.” It answers “why?”.
examples: I like this café because it’s quiet.
She left early because she was tired.
vocab.colloc: because of · just because

vocab.def: fairly, quite — a softener before an adjective.
vocab.use: As an adverb it means “quite”: “pretty good”. As an adjective it means attractive. Informal but very common.
examples: The film was pretty good.
It’s pretty cold today.
vocab.colloc: pretty good · pretty bad · pretty much

vocab.def: very, very much.
vocab.use: Goes before the adjective and is much stronger than “very”: “extremely expensive”. Not used with extreme adjectives like “terrible”.
examples: The service was extremely slow.
She’s extremely good at her job.
vocab.colloc: extremely useful · extremely rare

vocab.def: a formal way of saying “but”, joining two sentences.
vocab.use: It starts a new sentence and takes a comma: “The hotel was cheap. However, it was very noisy.”
examples: The food was great. However, the place was crowded.
However, nobody complained.
vocab.colloc: however, · however difficult

vocab.def: an informal “but”, often at the end of a sentence.
vocab.use: “It was expensive, though.” Also joins clauses at the start: “Though it rained, we went out.”
examples: I liked it. It was long, though.
Though he was tired, he finished the work.
vocab.colloc: even though · nice, though

vocab.def: slightly, a little — the weakest degree adverb.
vocab.use: Almost always with a negative adjective: “a bit expensive”, “a bit cold”. “A bit good” sounds wrong.
examples: The room was a bit small.
It’s a bit late to call her now.
vocab.colloc: a bit late · a bit noisy · just a bit

grammar.name: Adverbs before adjectives + conjunctions
grammar.short: really cheap, quite far — and, but, so, because.
grammar.rule: Adverbs of degree go directly in front of an adjective to make it stronger or weaker. Conjunctions join two ideas into one sentence, and each one shows a different relationship.
form: Degree: extremely > really / very > quite > a bit + adjective.
and (addition) · but (contrast) · so (result) · because (reason).
Order: idea + conjunction + idea → “It’s small but very comfortable.”
notes: “A bit” only works with negative adjectives: “a bit expensive”, not “a bit beautiful”.
“So” and “because” are opposites in direction: reason + so + result; result + because + reason.
Do not start a sentence with “because” alone in writing at this level — join it to the main idea.
examples: The restaurant is quite small but really nice.
It was cheap, so we bought two.
I love this park because it’s very quiet.
grammar.watch: “Very” cannot go with strong adjectives: not “very excellent” — just “excellent”.
grammar.deep: Adverbs of degree turn a flat adjective into an opinion with a temperature. Placed in front of the adjective, they run from weak to strong: somewhat, pretty, quite, very, really, extremely. Learning three or four of these will do more for how natural you sound than a page of new adjectives, because they let you agree politely (“it was pretty good”) or disagree strongly (“it was extremely expensive”) without changing the adjective itself. “Too” looks like the strongest of the family but does not belong to it at all: it means more than you want, so “too big” is always a complaint while “very big” can be praise. Conjunctions then join your evaluations together — and to add, but to contrast, however for a formal contrast, and though for a casual one, often thrown in at the end of the sentence.

chart.title: Degree adverbs and connectors
rows: It was too expensive for us.
It was cheap. However, it was noisy.

more: The hotel was really clean but a bit noisy.
The food is extremely good and quite cheap.
It rained all day, so we stayed inside.
I love that café because the coffee is excellent.
The beach was quite far, however the bus was easy.
It was a bit expensive, though.

fix.why: Strong adjectives already contain “very”; use “absolutely” if you need emphasis.
“Too” means more than you want, so it cannot introduce praise.

fix.wrong: Because the rain, we stayed in.
fix.right: Because it rained, we stayed in.
fix.why: “Because” needs a subject and a verb; “because of” takes a noun.

drill.name: Turn up the dial
drill.prompt: Say the same sentence five times, changing only the degree adverb: a bit → quite → very → really → extremely.

dialogue.line: How was the hostel?
Pretty good, actually. It was quite cheap and really clean.
Any problems?
It was a bit noisy at night, but it was close to everything, so it was worth it.

contrast.title: Degree and joining words
rows: It was late, so we left.
We left because it was late.
It was late. However, we stayed.

grammar.sound: “Quite” and “really” carry the stress, not the adjective: “It was REALLY good.” Flattening them makes praise sound like a complaint.

grammar.name: Modals “can” and “should” for recommendations
grammar.short: You can walk there. You should try the coffee.
grammar.rule: “Can” presents a possibility or an option; “should” gives advice — it is what you think is a good idea. Both are followed by the base verb, with no “to” and no -s.
form: You can + verb: You can take the bus from here.
You should + verb: You should visit the museum.
Negative: You shouldn’t go at night. Question: Should I book a table?
notes: No “to”: “You should go”, never “You should to go”.
“Shouldn’t” is a warning, not an order — it is softer than “don’t”.
“Could” is even softer than “can” for suggestions: “You could try the market.”
examples: You should try the arepas — they’re excellent.
You can pay by card in most shops.
You shouldn’t drive in the centre; it’s too crowded.
grammar.watch: Modals never take -s: “He should call”, not “He shoulds call”.
grammar.deep: “Can” and “should” do different jobs in advice and it is worth keeping them apart. “Can” presents an option — it tells the other person what is possible, and leaves the decision entirely with them: “You can take the metro; it’s faster.” “Should” presents a recommendation — your opinion about the best choice: “You should take the metro.” Both are modals, which means the same three mechanical rules apply: no -s in the third person, no “to” before the next verb, and no “do” in questions or negatives. So it is “She should call him”, “Should I call him?” and “You shouldn’t worry”. In practice English speakers soften advice by mixing the two: an option first, then a recommendation, which is why “You can wait, but I think you should call now” feels so natural.

chart.title: Can and should for recommendations
rows: the best idea in my opinion

more: You can pay by card here.
You should book a table at the weekend.
You shouldn’t drink the tap water.
Can I take photos inside? — Yes, you can.
Should we leave now or later?
You can walk, but I think you should take a taxi at night.

fix.wrong: You should to visit the museum.
fix.why: Modals are followed directly by the base verb, with no “to”.
Modals never take -s in the third person.
Modals make their own questions; “do” is not used.

drill.name: Option then advice
drill.prompt: For each situation give one option with “can” and one recommendation with “should”.
items: a visitor has one free day in your city
a classmate wants to improve listening
a tourist has lost their phone
someone wants cheap lunch near school

dialogue.line: I only have one day here. What should I do?
You should start at the old town — it’s the best part.
Can I walk there from the hotel?
You can, but it’s quite far. You should take the metro.

grammar.sound: In statements “can” is weak: /kən/. In short answers it is strong: “Yes, you CAN.” “Can’t” is always strong.

speaking.text: Recommend three places in your city to a visitor. Give a reason for each with “because”.
A tourist asks how to spend one day in your town. Answer with can and should.
Problem cards: each student reads a small problem, the others give advice with “You should…”.

tips: Adverbs of degree go before the adjective: “really cheap”.
“Should” + base verb, always without “to”.
“So” introduces a result; “because” introduces a reason.

quiz.q: You ___ visit the old town — it’s beautiful.
quiz.explain: Modals like “should” are followed directly by the base verb.

dynamics.name: Review roulette
dynamics.how: Each group gets a place card (a restaurant, a bus route, a park). They write a three-sentence review using one degree adverb, one contrast word and one recommendation. Cards rotate; the next group adds a disagreeing sentence.
dynamics.payoff: Every sentence has a required ingredient, and the disagreement forces “however” and “though”.

dynamics.name: Advice clinic
dynamics.how: Half the class writes a problem on a card and sits down; the other half circulates as advisers, giving one “can” option and one “should” recommendation per problem, then moving on.
dynamics.payoff: Repetition with variation — each adviser hears the same problem answered differently.

dynamics.name: Too or very
dynamics.how: The teacher reads a sentence with a gap; students hold up one of two cards, TOO or VERY, and one student justifies the choice.
dynamics.payoff: Fixes the single most persistent error in this unit in six minutes.

dynamics.name: City guide in three minutes
dynamics.how: Each group prepares a spoken mini-guide to their city for a visitor: three recommendations with “should”, two options with “can”, one warning with “shouldn’t”.
dynamics.payoff: Combines both grammar points in one product that can be presented and marked.

writing.title: An honest review
writing.brief: Write a short review of a place you know — a café, a park, a bus route. Give two positives and one negative, and finish with a recommendation. Use at least three different degree adverbs.
criteria: Three different degree adverbs, correctly placed before the adjective.
One contrast with “but”, “however” or “though”.
A final sentence with “should” or “shouldn’t”.

homework.title: Rewrite a real review
homework.task: Find a short online review in Spanish of a place near you. Rewrite it in English in six sentences, keeping the opinion but using at least three degree adverbs and one “should”. Mark your degree adverbs in bold.

test.q: The hotel was ___ expensive for us, so we left.
test.explain: “Too” means more than you want — a complaint, not praise.

test.q: You ___ book a table on Fridays.
test.explain: Modals take the base verb with no “to” and no -s.

test.q: It was cheap, ___ the room was tiny.
test.explain: The two ideas contrast, so “but” is the connector.
“Really” strengthens a positive adjective; “a bit” and “too” carry negative meaning.
Modals form their own questions by inversion.
