Beside it, TOO in a separate box marked “problem, not praise”.
A connector row: and · but · so · because · however · though.
Two model sentences: “You can walk there.” / “You should take the metro at night.”
Corner error: “You should to visit.”

units.title: WHAT SHOULD WE DO?
units.theme: Suggestions, requests and plans with other people

overview.intro: This unit is about making things happen together. You will recommend with infinitives, make suggestions, and ask for things politely with can, could and should — moving from direct to very polite.
goals: Make recommendations using infinitive structures.
Make suggestions and choose the right level of politeness.
Ask for help and permission with can, could and should.
overview.outcome: By the end you can plan an outing with a partner using three different suggestion patterns.

vocab.def: to offer an idea for other people to consider.
vocab.use: Patterns: suggest + -ing, or suggest that + clause. Never “suggest to do”.
examples: I suggest leaving early.
She suggested a different restaurant.
vocab.colloc: suggest an idea · suggest going

vocab.def: a thought or plan you can share.
vocab.use: Common replies: “Good idea!” / “That’s a great idea.”
examples: That’s a good idea.
I have an idea for Saturday.
vocab.colloc: a good idea · a bad idea · a great idea

vocab.def: to take something for a while / to give something for a while.
vocab.use: You borrow FROM someone; you lend TO someone. Do not swap them.
examples: Can I borrow your pen?
Could you lend me your charger?
vocab.colloc: borrow money · lend a hand · borrow a book

vocab.def: a kind action you do for someone.
vocab.use: Fixed phrase: “Can I ask you a favour?” US spelling: favor.
examples: Can you do me a favour?
She did me a big favour.
vocab.colloc: do a favour · ask a favour · a big favour

vocab.def: a short way to suggest doing something together.
vocab.use: “Let’s” + base verb: “Let’s go.” Negative: “Let’s not go.”
examples: Let’s meet at seven.
Let’s not take the car.
vocab.colloc: let’s go · let’s try · let’s see

vocab.def: perhaps, possibly.
vocab.use: It softens a suggestion: “Maybe we could eat first.” Usually at the start.
examples: Maybe we should call first.
Maybe next weekend.
vocab.colloc: maybe later · maybe not · maybe tomorrow

vocab.def: a friendly way of making a suggestion.
vocab.use: Followed by a base verb: “Why don’t we meet at six?” The answer is usually “Good idea” or “I’d rather not”.
examples: Why don’t we take a taxi?
Why don’t you ask your teacher?
vocab.colloc: why don’t we · why not · why don’t you try

vocab.def: another way of suggesting, followed by -ing or a noun.
vocab.use: “How about meeting at six?” or “How about Friday?” Never followed by an infinitive.
examples: How about going to the cinema?
How about a coffee after class?
vocab.colloc: how about tomorrow · what about you

vocab.def: in place of the other option.
vocab.use: At the end of the sentence alone (“Let’s stay in instead”) or as “instead of + noun/-ing”.
examples: The museum is closed, so let’s go to the park instead.
Instead of driving, we walked.
vocab.colloc: instead of that · go there instead

vocab.def: to like one option more than another.
vocab.use: “Prefer + to + verb” (“I prefer to walk”) or “prefer A to B” (“I prefer tea to coffee”).
examples: I prefer to meet in the morning.
Do you prefer this one or that one?
vocab.colloc: I’d prefer · prefer not to · prefer A to B

vocab.def: to be willing and happy to do something.
vocab.use: Informal, usually in questions: “Are you up for a coffee?” Followed by a noun or -ing.
examples: Are you up for a walk after class?
I’m up for anything tonight.
vocab.colloc: up for it · up for a coffee · not really up for

grammar.name: Recommendations with infinitives
grammar.short: It’s a good idea to book. Try to arrive early.
grammar.rule: Many recommendations in English use “to + verb” after a fixed phrase or after certain verbs. The infinitive keeps the advice general and polite.
form: It’s a good idea to + verb: It’s a good idea to book in advance.
The best way is to + verb: The best way is to walk.
want / need / try / hope / plan / decide + to + verb: You need to buy a ticket first.
notes: After “suggest” and “recommend” we use -ing, not “to”: “I recommend visiting the museum.”
After “should”, “can” and “could” there is no “to”.
“It’s better to…” and “It’s easier to…” follow the same pattern.
examples: It’s a good idea to arrive twenty minutes early.
You need to bring your ID.
The best way to see the city is to take the free tour.
grammar.watch: “Recommend to visit” is wrong; say “recommend visiting” or “I recommend that you visit”.
grammar.deep: Infinitive structures let you give advice without pointing at the person, which makes them the gentlest recommendations in English. Instead of “you should book early”, you can say “it’s a good idea to book early” or “the best thing to do is to book early”, and the advice becomes a general truth rather than an instruction. Grammatically these are all “to + base verb”, and the frames are fixed and worth memorising whole: it’s a good idea to…, it’s better to…, the best way to…, try to…. Two traps sit nearby. First, “recommend” and “suggest” do not take an object plus infinitive: say “I recommend booking early” or “I suggest that you book early”, never “I recommend you to book”. Second, “worth” takes -ing, not an infinitive: “it’s worth booking early”.

chart.title: Infinitive advice frames
rows: It’s a good idea to arrive early.
The best way to… is to…
The best way to learn is to practise.

more: It’s a good idea to arrive early.
The best way to learn is to speak every day.
You need to bring your ID to the exam.
I decided to take the later bus.
We’re planning to leave on Friday.
Try to write ten words a day.

fix.wrong: I recommend to visit the museum.
fix.why: “Recommend” takes -ing, not the infinitive.

fix.wrong: It’s a good idea booking early.
fix.right: It’s a good idea to book early.
fix.why: After “it’s a good idea” English uses “to + verb”.
“Not” goes before “to”, not between “to” and the verb.

drill.name: Same advice, three frames
drill.prompt: Give the same recommendation three ways: “It’s a good idea to…”, “The best way is to…”, “You need to…”.

dialogue.line: It’s my first time at the clinic. What do I do?
It’s a good idea to arrive twenty minutes early.
Do I need to bring anything?
You need to bring your ID. And try to eat something before you come.

contrast.title: to + verb or -ing?
rows: It’s a good idea to call.

grammar.sound: “To” is almost always weak: /tə/. “I need to go” has the stress on “need” and “go”, never on “to”.

grammar.name: Suggestions and requests with can, could and should
grammar.short: Can you…? Could you…? Should we…?
grammar.rule: These three modals cover suggestions and requests. “Can” is direct and friendly, “could” is more polite or more tentative, and “should” asks for or gives advice. All are followed by the base verb.
form: Request: Can you help me? / Could you help me, please? (more polite)
Permission: Can I sit here? / Could I use your phone?
Suggestion: Should we take a taxi? / We could walk. / Let’s walk.
notes: “Could” is not past here — it is politeness. Use it with strangers and in formal situations.
Answer a request with a verb, not just “yes”: “Of course.” / “Sure, no problem.”
“Shall we…?” is a more formal alternative to “Should we…?” in British English.
examples: Could you open the window, please?
Should we invite Ana too?
We could meet at the cinema instead.
grammar.watch: Add “please” to any request with “can” — without it, “Can you…?” can sound abrupt.
grammar.deep: “Can”, “could” and “should” cover almost every suggestion and request you will need, and the difference between them is social rather than logical. “Can you…?” is a direct, friendly request between people who know each other. “Could you…?” is one step more distant and therefore politer, which makes it the safest default with strangers, officials and anyone senior to you. “Should we…?” is not a request at all — it asks for a shared decision, so it belongs in group planning. Because these are modals, the mechanics never change: base verb after them, no “to”, no “do”. The one thing to add is a reason. English expects requests and refusals to come with an explanation, so “Could you send it today? I need it for the meeting” lands far better than the bare question.

chart.title: Can, could, should: requests and suggestions

more: Can you help me with this?
Could you say that again, please?
Should we take a taxi?
Could I use your phone for a second?
Why don’t we meet at the entrance?
Let’s book it now before the price changes.

fix.why: No “to” after a modal.

fix.wrong: How about to go to the cinema?
fix.right: How about going to the cinema?
fix.why: “How about” is followed by -ing or a noun.

fix.wrong: Why don’t we to leave early?
fix.why: “Why don’t we” is followed by the base verb.

drill.name: Politeness ladder
drill.prompt: Make the same request three times, from direct to very polite: Can you… → Could you… → Would you mind…

dialogue.line: Should we eat before the film or after?
Let’s eat before — the place next door is quick.
Could you book a table, then?
Sure. Can you buy the tickets while I call?

grammar.sound: Politeness lives in the melody, not the words. “Could you help me?” must rise at the end; flat intonation sounds like an order.

speaking.text: Plan a Saturday together. Each person must make at least three suggestions using a different pattern.
Ask a stranger, a colleague and a close friend for the same favour. Change the politeness each time.
Advice auction: read a travel problem, and the group votes for the best recommendation.

tips: “Could you…?” is the safest polite request in English.
“Recommend” and “suggest” take -ing, not “to”.
“Let’s” is only for things you do together.

quiz.q: ___ you pass me the salt, please?
quiz.explain: “Could you…, please?” is the standard polite request.

dynamics.name: Plan the weekend
dynamics.how: Each group must agree on a Saturday plan with a fixed budget. Every proposal must use a different suggestion form — no repeating “let’s”. The group writes the final plan in four lines.
dynamics.payoff: Forces variety across all the suggestion patterns instead of one favourite.

dynamics.name: Politeness ladder race
dynamics.how: Teacher calls a request. Pairs race to produce it at three politeness levels in order. First correct set scores.
dynamics.payoff: Makes the can/could/would mind distinction physical and fast.

dynamics.name: New in town
dynamics.how: Half the class are newcomers with a specific problem (no phone signal, no bank account, nowhere to eat late). The others give two recommendations each, using an infinitive frame at least once.
dynamics.payoff: Realistic content, and the infinitive frames get repeated across partners.

dynamics.name: Say it nicer
dynamics.how: Teacher reads a rude version (“Give me your pen.”). Students rewrite it politely on mini-whiteboards and hold it up together.
dynamics.payoff: Instant whole-class feedback on request forms.

writing.title: Advice for a visitor
writing.brief: A classmate from another city is coming for one day. Write them a message with three recommendations using infinitive frames and two suggestions for things to do together.
criteria: Two different infinitive frames (“it’s a good idea to…”, “the best way is to…”).
Two different suggestion forms (“let’s”, “why don’t we”, “how about”).
One polite request with “could”.

homework.title: Three messages, three registers
homework.task: Write the same request — asking someone to change a meeting time — three times: to a close friend, to a classmate, and to a teacher. Change the modal and the length, not the content.

test.explain: “It’s a good idea” is followed by “to + verb”.
“How about” is followed by -ing or a noun.

test.q: ___ you pass me the salt, please?
test.explain: “Could you…, please?” is the standard polite request.
“Recommend” takes the -ing form.
“Let’s” is followed by the base verb.

board: Two columns: TO + VERB (need, want, plan, hope, decide, it’s a good idea) | -ING (recommend, suggest, how about, worth).
A politeness ladder: Can you → Could you → Would you mind + -ing.
A suggestion row: Let’s · Why don’t we · How about · Should we.
A boxed model: “It’s a good idea to book. Why don’t we do it now?”
Corner error: “I recommend to visit.”

units.title: ME TOO, ME NEITHER
units.theme: Agreeing, disagreeing and making polite requests

overview.intro: This unit teaches the small phrases that keep a conversation alive: agreeing with “so” and “too”, agreeing with negatives using “neither” and “either”, and asking for things with “would”.
goals: Agree with positive and negative statements using so, too, neither and either.
Disagree politely without sounding rude.
Make requests and offers with would.
overview.outcome: By the end you can hold a two-minute conversation where you agree or disagree with everything your partner says.

vocab.def: to have the same opinion as someone.
vocab.use: “I agree with you.” Never “I am agree” — agree is a verb, not an adjective.
examples: I agree with you completely.
We don’t agree about politics.
vocab.colloc: agree with someone · totally agree · agree on a plan

vocab.def: the word for agreeing with a negative statement.
vocab.use: “Neither do I”, “Neither am I” — with inversion, and no extra “not”.
examples: I don’t like horror films. — Neither do I.
She isn’t coming. — Neither is he.
vocab.colloc: neither do I · neither am I · me neither

vocab.def: “also”, used at the end of a negative sentence.
vocab.use: “I don’t like it either.” In positive sentences we use “too”.
examples: I don’t drink coffee either.
He didn’t come either.
vocab.colloc: not… either · me either

vocab.def: what you think about something.
vocab.use: “In my opinion…” to introduce your view. Not “to my opinion”.
examples: In my opinion, it’s too expensive.
What’s your opinion?
vocab.colloc: in my opinion · a strong opinion · the same opinion

vocab.def: in fact — used to correct politely.
vocab.use: A soft way to disagree: “Actually, I think it’s quite good.”
examples: Actually, I don’t agree.
It’s actually cheaper online.
vocab.colloc: actually, I think · actually no

vocab.def: certainly — a friendly yes to a request.
vocab.use: Use it to accept a request: “Could you help me?” — “Of course.”
examples: Of course you can borrow it.
Of course, no problem.
vocab.colloc: of course · of course not

vocab.def: short ways of agreeing with a positive / a negative statement.
vocab.use: “I love coffee.” — “Me too.” / “I don’t like coffee.” — “Me neither.” They never change form.
examples: I’m tired. — Me too.
I can’t swim. — Me neither.
vocab.colloc: me too · me neither · same here

vocab.def: to have a different opinion.
vocab.use: “Disagree with someone about something”. In English it is polite to soften it: “I’m not sure I agree.”
examples: I disagree with that idea.
We disagreed about the price.
vocab.colloc: strongly disagree · agree to disagree

vocab.def: the standard way of introducing an opinion.
vocab.use: English puts the negative on “think”, not on the second verb: “I don’t think it’s a good idea.”
examples: I think this one is better.
I don’t think she knows.
vocab.colloc: I think so · I don’t think so · what do you think

vocab.def: correct / not correct.
vocab.use: With “to be”, not “have”: “You are right.” Never “You have reason”.
examples: You’re right — it starts at eight.
I was wrong about the date.
vocab.colloc: absolutely right · completely wrong · that’s right

vocab.def: to be annoyed or bothered by something.
vocab.use: “Would you mind + -ing?” is a polite request. The agreeing answer is negative: “Not at all.”
examples: Would you mind closing the door?
I don’t mind waiting.
vocab.colloc: would you mind · I don’t mind · never mind

vocab.def: a friendly “yes” to a request, or a reply to thanks.
vocab.use: Informal. With teachers or strangers, “Of course” or “Certainly” sounds better.
examples: “Could you help me?” — “No problem.”
“Thanks a lot.” — “No problem.”
vocab.colloc: no problem at all · that’s no problem

grammar.name: Agreeing and disagreeing with so, too, neither, either
grammar.short: So do I. / Me too. / Neither do I. / I don’t either.
grammar.rule: To agree with a positive statement use “so + helper + subject” or “… too”. To agree with a negative use “neither + helper + subject” or “… not … either”. The helper matches the verb in the first sentence.
form: Positive: “I love pizza.” → So do I. / I do too. / Me too.
Negative: “I don’t like fish.” → Neither do I. / I don’t either. / Me neither.
With “be”: “I’m tired.” → So am I. With modals: “I can swim.” → So can I.
notes: “So” and “neither” invert the word order: “So do I”, never “So I do”.
Never use two negatives: “Neither do I”, not “Neither don’t I”.
To disagree, use the opposite short answer: “I love fish.” — “Oh, I don’t.”
examples: I’m from Bogotá. — So am I.
I don’t eat meat. — Neither do I.
I went to the concert. — Really? I didn’t.
grammar.watch: Match the helper to the original sentence: “I have finished.” → “So have I”, not “So do I”.
grammar.deep: English hates repetition, so instead of saying “I also like coffee” it echoes only the skeleton of the other person’s sentence. That skeleton is the auxiliary: if your partner said “I have never been there”, your agreement is “Neither have I”, because their sentence was built on “have”. When a sentence has no auxiliary at all, “do” stands in: “I like it” gets “So do I”. Two more details finish the system. “So” and “neither” both require inversion — the verb comes before the subject, so “So do I” is right and “So I do” is not. And “neither” already carries the negative, which is why the verb after it stays positive. The informal versions, “me too” and “me neither”, never change shape and are perfectly acceptable in speech.
more: “I love this song.” — “So do I.”
“I’m tired.” — “So am I.”
“I don’t eat meat.” — “Neither do I.”
“I’ve never been to Chile.” — “Neither have I.”
“I went to the match.” — “Really? I didn’t.”
“I can’t swim.” — “I can’t either.”

fix.why: “So” agrees with positives; “neither” agrees with negatives.
The helper must match the original verb — “be” answers with “be”.
Choose one form: “Me neither” or “Neither do I”, never both.

drill.name: Match the helper
drill.prompt: Agree with each statement twice: once with so/neither, once with the short “Me too / Me neither”.

dialogue.line: I’m really tired today.
So am I. I didn’t sleep well.
Neither did I. And I don’t have any coffee at home.
I don’t either. Let’s buy one on the way.

contrast.title: Agreeing correctly
rows: Neither do I. / I don’t either.
Neither can I. / I can’t either.

grammar.sound: “So do I” has the stress on “I”. “Neither” can be /ˈnaɪðə/ or /ˈniːðə/ — both are correct; pick one and stay with it.

grammar.name: Requests with “would”
grammar.short: Would you mind…? I’d like… Would you like…?
grammar.rule: “Would” makes a request or an offer polite and indirect. It never changes form, and “I would” is usually shortened to “I’d”.
form: Offer: Would you like a coffee? Answer: Yes, please. / No, thank you.
Request: Would you mind closing the window? Answer: Not at all. / Of course not.
Want politely: I’d like the menu, please. / I’d rather stay home.
notes: After “would you mind” the verb takes -ing: “Would you mind waiting?”
Careful with the answer to “Would you mind…?”: “No, not at all” means yes, I will do it.
“I’d like” is a polite “I want” — always use it when ordering or asking.
examples: Would you like something to eat?
Would you mind helping me with this bag?
I’d like two tickets, please.
grammar.watch: “I would like” never takes -ing: “I’d like to go”, not “I’d like going”.
grammar.deep: “Would” turns an instruction into a request by moving it one step away from reality, and English reads that distance as respect. “Would you open the window?” asks about a hypothetical willingness rather than demanding an action, which is why it works with strangers, in shops and in emails. The related form “I would like” is your own polite wish, and it is the phrase to use when ordering or asking for something: “I’d like a coffee, please.” Keep three mechanics in mind. “Would” is a modal, so it is followed by a base verb with no “to”. Its contraction “’d” is everywhere in speech, so train your ear for it. And answers stay short and warm: “Of course”, “Certainly”, “Yes, please” — never a full repetition of the request.

chart.title: Requests with would
rows: Would you like to join us?
I’d like to book a table.

more: Would you like some water?
I’d like the chicken, please.
Would you mind waiting a moment?
Would you mind if I opened the window?
I’d rather sit outside, if that’s okay.
Would you like to join us?

fix.wrong: I would like to a coffee.
fix.why: “Would like” takes either a noun or “to + verb”, never both.
“Would you mind” is followed by -ing.

fix.wrong: “Would you mind opening the window?” — “Yes, of course.”
fix.right: “Would you mind opening the window?” — “Not at all.”
fix.why: The question asks whether it bothers you, so agreeing means answering no.

drill.name: Order and ask
drill.prompt: In a café: order with “I’d like”, then make one request with “Would you mind…?” and one with “Could you…?”.

dialogue.line: Good evening. Would you like a table inside or outside?
Outside, please. Would you mind moving that chair?
Not at all. Would you like to see the menu?
Yes, please. And I’d like a glass of water while I decide.

contrast.title: Would in offers and requests
rows: Not at all. / Of course not.

grammar.sound: “Would you” blends to /wʊdʒə/. Practise “Would you mind…?” as two beats so it sounds like an offer, not an interrogation.

speaking.text: Agreement chain: one student makes a statement, the next agrees with so/neither, the next disagrees politely.
Compare tastes in food, music and films. Use “So do I” and “Neither do I” at least six times.
You are neighbours making polite requests to each other with “Would you mind…?”.

tips: Positive agreement → so / too. Negative agreement → neither / either.
“So” and “neither” invert: helper before subject.
“Would you mind + -ing” — never the base verb.

quiz.explain: To agree with a negative statement we use “Neither do I”.

dynamics.name: Agreement ladder
dynamics.how: Two lines face each other. Line A makes a true statement; Line B must agree correctly within three seconds. Wrong helper means stepping back. Lines shift one place every round.
dynamics.payoff: Speed forces automatic helper-matching, which is the whole point of this grammar.

dynamics.name: Café roleplay with obstacles
dynamics.how: One waiter, two customers. The teacher hands the waiter secret obstacle cards (no tables outside, kitchen closing). Every request must be polite; every refusal must be softened.
dynamics.payoff: Real pressure on “would” forms, and the obstacles generate re-requests.

dynamics.name: Find three things in common
dynamics.how: Pairs must find three things in common and three differences, reporting each with a so/neither/either answer. Then they change partners and report the previous pair’s results.
dynamics.payoff: The reporting stage recycles the structures with third-person content.

dynamics.name: Mind the request
dynamics.how: Teacher makes a “Would you mind…?” request. Students answer with thumbs and the correct phrase. Anyone who says “Yes, of course” to mean agreement explains the trap.
dynamics.payoff: Kills the most common answer error in one short round.

writing.title: A conversation on paper
writing.brief: Write a dialogue of ten lines between two friends deciding where to eat. Include three agreements (so/neither/either), one polite request with “would”, and one disagreement.
criteria: Every agreement uses a helper that matches the original sentence.
At least one “Would you mind + -ing” with a correct answer.
The disagreement uses the opposite helper: “Really? I don’t.”

homework.title: Agreement diary
homework.task: During one day, note five things people say to you in any language. Write each one in English and write the agreement or disagreement you would give in English. Bring the five pairs to class.

test.q: “I don’t like horror films.” — “___ do I.”
test.explain: Agreeing with a negative uses “Neither do I”.
The helper must match “to be”: “So am I.”
“Would you mind” is followed by the -ing form.
Agreeing to a “mind” question means saying no.
“Either” goes at the end of a negative agreement.

board: Two facing columns: POSITIVE → So + helper + I | NEGATIVE → Neither + helper + I.
A helper key underneath: be → am/is/are · do → do/does · past → did · perfect → have · modal → can.
A “would” box: Would you like…? · I’d like… · Would you mind + -ing.
The trap answer in a circle: “Not at all.” = yes.
Corner error: “I don’t like coffee.” — “So do I.”

units.title: BIGGEST AND FARTHEST

overview.intro: This unit takes you around the world. You will compare two places with comparatives, name the number one with superlatives, and ask about size, height, depth and temperature with “how”.
goals: Form and use superlatives with the and -est or the most.
Describe geography: mountains, rivers, deserts, coasts.
Ask about measurements with how long, how tall, how high, how deep.
overview.outcome: By the end you can present a country or region with three comparatives and three superlatives.

vocab.def: a very high natural rise of land.
vocab.use: A group is a “mountain range”. We say “in the mountains” for the area.
examples: The Andes are the longest mountain range in the world.
We spent the weekend in the mountains.
vocab.colloc: a high mountain · climb a mountain · mountain range

vocab.def: the land next to the sea.
vocab.use: “On the coast” for a place: “Santa Marta is on the coast.”
examples: My family lives on the Caribbean coast.
The coast is warmer than the capital.
vocab.colloc: on the coast · the north coast · a rocky coast

vocab.def: going a long way down.
vocab.use: Question: “How deep is it?” Noun: depth.
examples: This lake is very deep.
How deep is the river here?
vocab.colloc: deep water · very deep · ten metres deep

vocab.def: the number of people living in a place.
vocab.use: Singular verb: “The population is growing.” Not “are”.
examples: The population of Bogotá is about eight million.
It has a small population.
vocab.colloc: a large population · the total population

vocab.def: with little water in the air / with a lot of water in the air.
vocab.use: Weather adjectives. Say “It’s humid”, not “There is humid”.
examples: The desert is very dry.
The coast is hotter and more humid.
vocab.colloc: a dry season · very humid · dry weather

vocab.def: used to make a superlative much stronger.
vocab.use: Before or after the superlative: “It’s by far the biggest city.”
examples: It’s by far the best beach in the country.
She is by far the fastest runner.
vocab.colloc: by far the best · by far the largest

vocab.def: a long stream of water / a large area of water surrounded by land.
vocab.use: With “the” for named rivers (the Magdalena) but not for lakes (Lake Titicaca).
examples: The Amazon is the longest river in South America.
We swam in the lake.
vocab.colloc: a wide river · cross the river · a deep lake

vocab.def: a very dry region / a very wet, dense forest.
vocab.use: Careful with the pronunciation of “desert” (dry place) and “dessert” (sweet food).
examples: The desert is extremely dry.
Colombia has a huge area of rainforest.
vocab.colloc: a hot desert · tropical rainforest

vocab.def: the top of the group.
vocab.use: Superlatives always take “the”: “the highest mountain”. Long adjectives take “the most”: “the most beautiful”.
examples: It’s the highest building in the city.
That’s the most expensive option.
vocab.colloc: the biggest · the most popular · one of the best

vocab.def: units of length and distance.
vocab.use: Used in measurement answers: “two metres tall”, “ten kilometres away”. US spelling: meter, kilometer.
examples: The wall is three metres high.
The airport is twenty kilometres from here.
vocab.colloc: square metres · a few kilometres away

vocab.def: two times bigger, longer or more than something else.
vocab.use: “Twice as long as”, “three times as expensive as”. The adjective stays in its base form.
examples: The Amazon is more than twice as long as the Magdalena.
This flat is twice as expensive as mine.
vocab.colloc: twice as big · three times as many · half as long

vocab.def: approximately, about.
vocab.use: Goes before the number: “roughly 200 kilometres”. Synonyms: about, around, approximately.
examples: It’s roughly two hours by bus.
The lake is roughly 40 metres deep.
vocab.colloc: roughly the same · roughly 300 metres

grammar.name: Comparatives and superlatives
grammar.short: bigger than / the biggest in the world.
grammar.rule: Comparatives compare two things; superlatives pick out the number one in a group. Short adjectives take -er / the -est; long adjectives take more / the most.
form: Short: hot → hotter → the hottest; easy → easier → the easiest.
Long: expensive → more expensive → the most expensive.
Irregular: good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst; far → further → the furthest.
notes: Superlatives always take “the”: “the highest mountain”, never “highest mountain”.
After a superlative use “in” for places and “of” for groups: “the biggest city in Colombia”, “the tallest of the three”.
Never double the marker: “the most biggest” is wrong.
examples: The Amazon is longer than the Magdalena.
Bogotá is the largest city in Colombia.
This is by far the most beautiful beach on the coast.
grammar.watch: Comparative + “than”; superlative + “the” + “in/of”. Mixing them is the most common error here.
grammar.deep: Comparatives and superlatives are built from the same two families you met in unit 3, and the split is still about length. Short adjectives add -er and -est: cheap, cheaper, the cheapest. Long adjectives take “more” and “the most”: expensive, more expensive, the most expensive. The superlative always keeps “the”, because it identifies one unique item, and it is normally followed by a phrase that names the group: “the biggest city in Colombia”, “the best day of my life”. Two useful extras: “one of the + superlative + plural noun” lets you praise without claiming first place (“one of the most beautiful cities”), and intensifiers such as “by far” and “much” let you show how big the gap is (“by far the largest”, “much cheaper”).
more: The Pacific is deeper than the Atlantic.
Bogotá is the coldest big city in Colombia.
This is the most beautiful beach on the coast.
My town is smaller than yours but much quieter.
Chocó is by far the wettest region in the country.
Today is the worst day of the week for traffic.

fix.wrong: Bogotá is the most cold city.
fix.why: One-syllable adjectives take -est, not “most”.

fix.wrong: It’s the biggest city of Colombia.
fix.right: It’s the biggest city in Colombia.
fix.why: With places the superlative takes “in”, not “of”.
“Better” is already comparative; never add “more”.

drill.name: Two then one
drill.prompt: Compare the first two items, then name the number one of the three.
items: the bus / the metro / a taxi — fast
your town / this city / the capital — noisy

dialogue.line: Which is bigger, Medellín or Cali?
Medellín, I think. But Bogotá is much bigger than both.
So Bogotá is the biggest city in the country?
By far. It’s roughly three times as big as Medellín.

grammar.sound: “-er than” runs together as /ərðən/: “bigger than” is two beats. “The most” keeps “the” weak: /ðəˈməʊst/.

grammar.name: Questions with “how” about measurements
grammar.short: How long? How tall? How high? How deep?
grammar.rule: For measurements English uses “how” plus the adjective. The answer usually gives a number plus the unit, and often repeats the adjective.
form: How long is it? — It’s about 200 kilometres long.
How tall is he? / How high is the mountain? — It’s 5,000 metres high.
How deep / how cold / how hot is it? — It’s ten metres deep. / It’s 30 degrees.
notes: “Tall” for people and thin things; “high” for mountains, walls and prices.
The unit comes before the adjective in the answer: “two metres deep”, not “deep two metres”.
“How far” asks about distance: “How far is the coast?” — “About four hours by bus.”
examples: How high is Monserrate? — Around 3,150 metres.
How long is the Magdalena River?
How hot is it in summer? — Usually about 32 degrees.
grammar.watch: Do not use “how much” for size: it is “How tall”, “How long”, “How far” — not “How much tall”.
grammar.deep: To ask about a measurement, English builds a question from “how” plus the relevant adjective, and the adjective tells you which dimension you mean: how long for length or duration, how tall for people and buildings, how high for mountains and walls, how deep for water, how wide for roads and rivers. The answer follows a fixed shape that reverses the order of the question: number, unit, adjective — “two metres deep”, “eighty kilometres long”. This is worth practising because it is the opposite of what most learners produce at first. Note also that some of these adjectives have their own nouns for the measurement — length, height, depth, width — which are useful when you need to be formal: “What is the height of the building?”

chart.title: How + adjective for measurements
rows: It’s ten metres long. / two hours long.

more: How long is the river? — About 6,400 kilometres long.
How high is Monserrate? — Roughly 3,150 metres high.
How deep is the lake? — Around 40 metres deep.
How far is the airport? — About twenty minutes away.
How tall is your brother? — One metre eighty.
How cold does it get in January? — Around eight degrees.

fix.wrong: How much long is the river?
fix.why: “How” combines directly with the adjective.
Measurements use “to be”, and the adjective repeats at the end.
People are tall; mountains and buildings are high.

drill.name: Ask the measurement
drill.prompt: Ask about each item with the right “how” question, then answer with a number and the repeated adjective.
items: the tallest building in your city

dialogue.line: How far is Villa de Leyva from here?
Roughly 160 kilometres — about three hours by car.
And how high is it?
Around 2,100 metres. It’s a bit colder than Bogotá at night.

grammar.sound: Numbers are the stressed word in the answer: “It’s about TWO HUNDRED kilometres long.” Say large numbers in groups, not digit by digit.

speaking.text: Compare two regions of your country: climate, population, food and cost. Use three comparatives each.
Superlative quiz: write five “What is the …est …?” questions about geography and test another pair.
Present your favourite place in one minute using at least two superlatives.

tips: Superlatives need “the”: the biggest, the most expensive.
Say the unit first: “ten metres deep”.
“Tall” for people, “high” for mountains.

quiz.q: The Amazon is ___ river in the world.
quiz.explain: A superlative needs “the” + -est: “the longest river in the world”.

dynamics.name: Record breakers
dynamics.how: Each group writes five superlative claims about the world, two of them false. Groups swap sheets and mark true or false, correcting the language errors they find as they go.
dynamics.payoff: Content is interesting enough to argue about, and peer correction catches “the most big”.

dynamics.name: Guess the measurement
dynamics.how: Teacher shows a photo of a place. Students write a guess for three measurements (height, length, distance) as full sentences. Closest full correct sentence wins the round.
dynamics.payoff: Only correct question and answer forms score, so accuracy matters more than the guess.

dynamics.name: Two cities, one winner
dynamics.how: Each student defends one city with five comparative sentences. Their partner must respond to each one with a counter-comparative before adding their own.
dynamics.payoff: Chains of comparatives with real disagreement to fuel them.

dynamics.name: Superlative line-up
dynamics.how: Students line up by a criterion the teacher calls (distance travelled to school, hours slept). Then the class describes the line with superlatives and comparatives.
dynamics.payoff: Physical ordering makes the superlative meaning literal and visible.

writing.title: Three places, one paragraph
writing.brief: Compare three places you know — your town, a place you have visited, and a place you want to visit. Use two comparatives, two superlatives and two measurements.
criteria: Comparatives use “than”; superlatives use “the” and “in”.
Two measurement sentences with a number and the repeated adjective.
No double comparatives (“more better”).

homework.title: Fact file
homework.task: Build a fact file on one river, one mountain and one city: length, height and population. Write six sentences comparing them, and check your numbers against two sources before class.

test.q: The Amazon is ___ river in the world.
test.explain: A superlative needs “the” + -est.

test.q: Bogotá is the biggest city ___ Colombia.
test.explain: Superlatives with places use “in”.

test.q: How ___ is the mountain? — About 5,000 metres.
test.explain: Mountains are high; people are tall.
Long adjectives form the comparative with “more” + “than”.

test.q: My town is ___ as big as yours.
test.explain: The structure is “twice as + adjective + as”.

board: Three columns: ADJECTIVE | COMPARATIVE | SUPERLATIVE, filled with big, easy, expensive, good, bad, far.
A rule strip: short → -er / the -est · long → more / the most.
A “how” family list: long · tall · high · deep · far · cold.
A boxed answer model: “It’s about 200 kilometres long.”
Corner errors: “the most big” and “more better”.

units.title: PLANS AND MESSAGES
units.theme: Future arrangements and passing messages on

overview.intro: This unit looks forward. You will talk about plans with “be going to” and about fixed arrangements with the present continuous, and then learn to pass a message on with “tell” and “say”.
goals: Talk about intentions and arrangements in the future.
Choose between be going to and the present continuous.
Report messages correctly with tell and say and make requests with modals.
overview.outcome: By the end you can describe your plans for next week and leave a clear message for someone who is not there.

vocab.def: to decide what you are going to do.
vocab.use: Verb: “plan to travel” (with “to”). Noun: “make plans”.
examples: We’re planning to travel in December.
Do you have plans for the weekend?
vocab.colloc: make plans · plan a trip · change plans

vocab.def: a fixed time to see a doctor, dentist or professional.
vocab.use: “Have an appointment”, “make an appointment”. Not for meeting friends — that is “meet up”.
examples: I have a doctor’s appointment at four.
Can I make an appointment for Friday?
vocab.colloc: make an appointment · a dentist appointment

vocab.def: information you leave for someone who is not there.
vocab.use: “Leave a message”, “give someone a message”, “take a message”.
examples: Can I leave a message?
I got your message this morning.
vocab.colloc: leave a message · take a message · send a message

vocab.def: to return someone’s phone call.
vocab.use: Separable with a pronoun: “call me back”, not “call back me”.
examples: Could you tell her to call me back?
I’ll call you back in ten minutes.
vocab.colloc: call back later · call me back

vocab.def: having a lot to do; not free.
vocab.use: “Busy with something” or “busy + -ing”: “She’s busy working.”
examples: I’m busy on Tuesday morning.
He’s busy studying for an exam.
vocab.colloc: very busy · busy week · too busy

vocab.def: going to do something in the next few minutes.
vocab.use: Followed by the base verb: “I’m about to leave.”
examples: I’m about to start dinner.
The film is about to begin.
vocab.colloc: just about to · about to leave

vocab.def: the form for plans you have already decided.
vocab.use: “Be going to + base verb”: “I’m going to study tonight.” Not “I’m going to study” for a spontaneous decision — that takes “will”.
examples: We’re going to move next month.
What are you going to do at the weekend?
vocab.colloc: going to start · going to be late

vocab.def: to give information for someone who is not there.
vocab.use: Fixed phrase: “Can I leave a message?” The person who receives it “takes a message”.
examples: She isn’t here — can I take a message?
I left a message on his phone.
vocab.colloc: leave a message · take a message

vocab.def: free and able to talk or meet.
vocab.use: For people and times: “She isn’t available right now”, “Is Friday available?”
examples: He’s not available until three.
Are you available tomorrow morning?
vocab.colloc: available now · not available · availability

vocab.def: to make someone remember something.
vocab.use: “Remind someone to + verb”: “Remind me to call her.” Different from “remember”, which is your own memory.
examples: Please remind me to send the file.
She reminded me about the meeting.
vocab.colloc: remind me to · a reminder · gently remind

vocab.def: to be later than planned, with the delay still happening.
vocab.use: Always continuous: “I’m running late.” Not “I run late” for one occasion.
examples: Sorry, I’m running a bit late.
She called to say she’s running late.
vocab.colloc: running late · running ten minutes late

vocab.def: to collect a person or thing from a place.
vocab.use: Separable: “pick me up”, “pick up the tickets”. With a pronoun, it must split.
examples: I’m picking my sister up at six.
Could you pick up the keys on your way?
vocab.colloc: pick someone up · pick up a package

grammar.name: Future with “be going to” and the present continuous
grammar.short: I’m going to study. I’m meeting Ana at six.
grammar.rule: “Be going to” expresses an intention or a prediction. The present continuous expresses a fixed arrangement, usually with a time and a place already decided.
form: be going to + base verb: I’m going to look for a new job.
Present continuous for arrangements: We’re flying on Sunday at nine.
Negative and question: She isn’t going to come. Are you going to study tonight?
notes: Both forms need “to be” — do not drop it: “I going to travel” is wrong.
Use “going to” for a plan without details; use the continuous when it is already booked.
Time words help: tomorrow, next week, on Friday, tonight.
examples: I’m going to study medicine next year.
We’re meeting the teacher at four on Friday.
Are you going to call her tonight?
grammar.watch: Avoid “I’m going to go”-style repetition when you can: “I’m going to the cinema” is enough for arrangements.
grammar.deep: “Be going to” and the present continuous both talk about the future, and both contain a present tense, which is exactly why they feel so certain: the plan already exists as you speak. The difference is how fixed it is. “Be going to” expresses an intention — you have decided, but the details may still move: “I’m going to look for a new job.” The present continuous expresses an arrangement — the time, the place or the other people are already settled: “I’m meeting the client at four.” This is why diaries are written in the present continuous and ambitions in “going to”. A time expression is almost always necessary with the continuous, otherwise your listener will hear it as “right now” instead of “later”, so keep “tomorrow”, “on Friday” or “at six” in the sentence.

chart.title: Two ways of talking about the future
rows: I’m going to start a course.
Look at the sky — it’s going to rain.

more: I’m going to look for a new job next year.
We’re flying to Lima on Sunday at nine.
She isn’t going to come — she has to work.
Are you going to tell him tonight?
I’m meeting the dentist at four on Thursday.
It’s going to rain — look at those clouds.

fix.wrong: I go to study medicine next year.
fix.right: I’m going to study medicine next year.
fix.why: An intention needs “be going to”, not the present simple.

fix.wrong: We going to travel in July.
fix.right: We’re going to travel in July.
fix.why: Never drop “am / is / are” from the future forms.

fix.wrong: I will meet Ana tomorrow at six — it’s arranged.
fix.right: I’m meeting Ana tomorrow at six.
fix.why: A fixed arrangement with a time and place takes the present continuous.

drill.name: Intention or arrangement
drill.prompt: Say each plan twice: once as an intention with “going to”, once as a fixed arrangement with the present continuous.

dialogue.line: What are you doing on Saturday?
I’m meeting my cousin at the station at ten. Then we’re going to look for a present for my mother.
Are you going to be back by six?
I think so. Why — is something happening?

grammar.sound: “Going to” becomes /ˈɡənə/ in speech. Understand it at speed even if you say the full form yourself.

grammar.name: Messages with “tell” and “say” + requests with modals
grammar.short: Tell him to call. Say that you’re late.
grammar.rule: “Tell” needs a person straight after it; “say” does not. For messages we often combine them with a modal request: can, could or would.
form: tell + person + (to + verb / that + clause): Tell Ana to call me. / Tell her that I’m late.
say + (that) + clause / say something to someone: Say that you’re sorry. / She said hello to me.
Requests: Could you tell him I called? / Can you say that again, please?
notes: Never “say me” — it is “tell me” or “say to me”.
“Tell” + person + “to” + verb turns an order into a message: “Tell him to wait.”
In messages the reporting verb is often in the past: “She said she was busy.”
examples: Could you tell her that the meeting is at ten?
Tell him to call me back after six.
Can you say that again more slowly, please?
grammar.watch: “Tell” always needs a person; “say” usually needs the words. “He told that…” and “He said me…” are both wrong.
grammar.deep: “Say” and “tell” carry the same information and different grammar, and one small rule separates them: “tell” must be followed by the person, “say” must not. So it is “She told me she was late” and “She said she was late”, never “She said me”. If you really want a person after “say”, you have to insert “to”: “she said to me”. When you pass a message on, the tense usually shifts one step back, because the words were spoken before you repeat them: “I’ll call later” becomes “He said he would call later”. Around this sit the request modals — can, could and would — which decide how polite the original message sounded, and it is worth keeping that level when you report it, because reporting a polite request as an order changes the whole picture.

chart.title: Say, tell and passing on messages
rows: She said to me that she was busy.
She told me she was busy.
“I’ll call.” → He said he would call.

more: Could you tell her that I called?
Tell him to wait outside.
She said she was busy this afternoon.
Can you say that again, please?
Tell them the meeting is at ten.
He told me to bring my passport.

fix.why: “Say” does not take a person directly; “tell” does.

fix.wrong: She told that she was late.
fix.right: She said that she was late.
fix.why: “Tell” needs a person before the clause: “She told me that…”.
A message with an instruction needs “to + verb”.

drill.name: Pass it on
drill.prompt: Hear a message, then pass it on with “tell” and again with “say”.
items: The meeting has moved to Friday.

dialogue.line: Hello, is Marcela there?
She’s out. Can I take a message?
Could you tell her that Andrés called? And tell her to check her email.
Of course. I’ll say you called at four.

contrast.title: tell vs say
rows: She said that she was tired.

grammar.sound: In messages, the important word is the content, not the verb: “Tell her the meeting is at TEN.” Keep “tell her” fast and quiet.

speaking.text: Compare your diaries for next week. Find one time when you are both free.
Phone call: the person you want is not there. Leave a message; your partner repeats it back.
Tell your partner three plans for this year and three arrangements already fixed.

tips: “Going to” = intention. Present continuous = already arranged.
“Tell” + person; “say” + words.
Never drop “am/is/are” in the future forms.

quiz.q: Could you ___ her that I called?
quiz.explain: “Tell” is followed directly by the person: “tell her that…”.

dynamics.name: Diary clash
dynamics.how: Each student gets a filled diary for next week and must find two hours when both are free, asking only about arrangements. No showing the paper.
dynamics.payoff: Sustained present continuous for arrangements with a genuine information gap.

dynamics.name: Broken telephone, message edition
dynamics.how: The first student reads a written message. It is passed down the row orally using “tell” and “say”, and the last student writes it on the board for comparison with the original.
dynamics.payoff: The distortions expose exactly where the reporting structures break.

dynamics.name: Fortune teller
dynamics.how: Student A makes six predictions about B’s next five years with “going to”. B accepts or rejects each one with a reason.
dynamics.payoff: Prediction sense of “going to” gets equal time with the intention sense.

dynamics.name: The office phone
dynamics.how: One caller, one receptionist, one absent colleague. The caller leaves a three-part message; the receptionist writes it and reports it to the colleague when they return.
dynamics.payoff: The message survives two transformations, which is the real-world version of this grammar.

writing.title: Message and plan
writing.brief: Write two short texts. First, a message to a classmate passing on something a teacher told you. Second, four lines about your plans for next month: two intentions and two fixed arrangements.
criteria: Correct “tell + person” and “say + words” in the message.
Two “going to” sentences and two present-continuous arrangements.
Every future form keeps am / is / are.

homework.title: Next month, on paper
homework.task: Write your real diary for the next two weeks in English, marking each entry as a plan or an arrangement. Then record a 45-second voice note describing three of them, using the correct form for each.

test.q: Could you ___ her that I called?
test.explain: “Tell” is followed directly by the person.

test.q: We ___ at nine on Sunday — the tickets are booked.
test.explain: A fixed arrangement with time and place uses the present continuous.

test.q: Look at those clouds. It ___ rain.
test.explain: A prediction based on evidence uses “be going to”.
“Tell + person + to + verb” carries an instruction.
Without a person, the verb is “say”: “She said (that) she was busy.”

board: A calendar strip for next week with two entries circled: one plan, one arrangement.
Two boxes: GOING TO = intention / prediction | PRESENT CONTINUOUS = fixed arrangement.
A tell/say split: tell + PERSON | say + WORDS.
A boxed model: “Could you tell her that the meeting is at ten?”
Corner errors: “He said me” and “We going to travel”.

units.title: HOW LIFE CHANGES
units.theme: Comparing past and present, and looking ahead

overview.intro: The final unit brings all your tenses together. You will describe how you and your city have changed — past simple for finished events, present simple for now, present perfect for results — and then look forward with verbs plus infinitives.
goals: Choose the right tense to describe change: past simple, present simple, present perfect.
Compare your past self with your present self.
Express hopes and plans with verb + infinitive patterns.
overview.outcome: By the end you can talk for two minutes about how your life has changed and what you hope to do next.

vocab.def: to become different.
vocab.use: Both verb and noun: “The city has changed.” / “a big change”.
examples: My neighbourhood has changed a lot.
I want to change jobs.
vocab.colloc: change a lot · a big change · change your mind

vocab.def: to become an adult; to spend your childhood somewhere.
vocab.use: Usually in the past: “I grew up in Cali.” Irregular: grow → grew → grown.
examples: I grew up in a small town.
My children are growing up fast.
vocab.colloc: grow up in a city · grow up together

vocab.def: a past habit that is now finished.
vocab.use: “I used to play football” — always with the base verb, and only about the past.
examples: I used to live with my parents.
She used to smoke, but she stopped.
vocab.colloc: used to be · used to have · didn’t use to

vocab.def: to want something good to happen.
vocab.use: Pattern: hope + to + verb, or hope + that + clause.
examples: I hope to finish university next year.
I hope you feel better soon.
vocab.colloc: hope to travel · hope so · I hope not

vocab.def: something you want to achieve.
vocab.use: “Set a goal”, “reach a goal”. Also “my goal is to + verb”.
examples: My goal is to speak English fluently.
She reached all her goals this year.
vocab.colloc: set a goal · reach a goal · a long-term goal

vocab.def: at the present time, compared with the past.
vocab.use: Usually at the start or end of a sentence, with the present simple.
examples: Nowadays I work from home.
People travel more nowadays.
vocab.colloc: nowadays people · much easier nowadays

vocab.def: to get better, or to make something better.
vocab.use: Works with and without an object: “My English has improved” and “I want to improve my English”.
examples: My pronunciation has improved a lot.
We need to improve the service.
vocab.colloc: improve quickly · a big improvement

vocab.def: now, in contrast with the past.
vocab.use: Always with a present tense: “These days I work from home.” Sits at the start or the end.
examples: These days everyone pays with a phone.
I don’t go out much these days.
vocab.colloc: these days · not these days

vocab.def: to choose after thinking about it.
vocab.use: “Decide to + verb” (“I decided to move”) or “decide on + noun” (“We decided on Friday”). Never “decide + -ing”.
examples: I’ve decided to change jobs.
We haven’t decided yet.
vocab.colloc: decide to go · a big decision · make a decision

vocab.def: to feel happy about something in the future.
vocab.use: Followed by a noun or -ing, never an infinitive: “I look forward to seeing you.”
examples: I’m looking forward to the weekend.
She’s looking forward to starting her new job.
vocab.colloc: look forward to hearing from you · really looking forward to it

vocab.def: at that time in the past.
vocab.use: Used with the past simple, usually at the start or end: “Back then, we had no internet.”
examples: Back then, everyone walked to school.
We were much younger back then.
vocab.colloc: back then · way back then

vocab.def: to arrive at a final situation you did not plan.
vocab.use: Followed by -ing or a place: “I ended up studying law.” Usually in the past.
examples: I ended up living in Bogotá for six years.
We ended up at a small café near the park.
vocab.colloc: end up doing · end up somewhere

grammar.name: Comparing tenses: past simple, present simple, present perfect
grammar.short: I lived / I live / I have lived — which one?
grammar.rule: Each tense has one job. The past simple describes a finished period. The present simple describes the situation now. The present perfect describes a change or result that connects the past to now.
form: Past simple + finished time: I lived in Cali until 2018.
Present simple + now / nowadays: I live in Bogotá now.
Present perfect + already / never / so far / in my life: The city has grown a lot.
notes: Present perfect with “for” and “since” describes something still true: “I have lived here for five years.”
“Used to + verb” is the clearest way to describe an old habit that has stopped.
Keep one time frame per sentence — do not mix “yesterday” with the present perfect.
examples: I used to take the bus, but now I walk.
My city has changed a lot in ten years.
I studied French at school, but I don’t speak it now.
grammar.watch: “I have lived here in 2015” is wrong. With a finished date, use the past simple: “I lived here in 2015.”
grammar.deep: Talking about change means running three time frames in the same paragraph, and each clause needs its own tense and its own time marker. Use “used to” or the past simple for what is no longer true, the present simple for the current situation, and the present perfect as the bridge that links them: “I used to smoke. I’ve stopped now. These days I run twice a week.” The present perfect is the key piece, because its whole job is to connect a past event to the present result, which is precisely what a story of change needs. Two habits help. Keep the subject and the topic constant so the tense shift is the only thing moving, and put a visible connector at every shift — “but now”, “these days”, “since then” — or your listener will hear the present sentence as part of the past.

chart.title: Describing change across tenses
rows: I used to live with my parents.
I’m staying with a friend this month.
I’m going to buy a flat.

more: I used to take the bus, but now I walk.
My city has changed a lot in ten years.
I studied French at school, but I don’t speak it now.
She’s lived here since 2019.
Back then there were no cafés on this street; now there are six.
I’ve worked in three cities, and I ended up here.

fix.why: A finished date forces the past simple.
The positive form is always “used to”, with the -d.
After “did”, the verb goes back to “use”.

drill.name: Then, now, since
drill.prompt: Say three sentences on one topic: how it was (past simple or used to), how it is (present simple), and what has changed (present perfect).

dialogue.line: Has the neighbourhood changed much?
A lot. There used to be a market here.
When did it close?
In 2017, I think. Since then they’ve built two blocks of flats.

contrast.title: Choosing the tense
rows: I’ve lived here for five years.

grammar.sound: “Used to” is pronounced /ˈjuːstə/ — the d disappears completely. Practise “I used to live” as three quick beats.

grammar.name: Verbs + infinitives for plans
grammar.short: going to, hope to, want to, would like to.
grammar.rule: To talk about the future you often need a verb followed by “to + base verb”. Each verb adds a different level of certainty, from a firm plan to a distant wish.
form: Certain: I’m going to start a new course in March.
Likely: I plan to / I want to / I need to move next year.
Less certain / polite: I hope to travel abroad. / I’d like to study design.
notes: “Would like to” is more polite and more tentative than “want to”.
After “hope”, “plan”, “want”, “need”, “decide” and “would like” we always use “to + verb”.
To be negative, put “not” before “to”: “I decided not to change jobs.”
examples: I’m going to finish this course in December.
I hope to work abroad one day.
I’d like to learn another language after English.
grammar.watch: Do not use -ing after these verbs: “I hope to travel”, never “I hope travelling”.
grammar.deep: A large group of everyday verbs is followed by “to + base verb”, and most of them share one idea: they point forwards at something not yet real. You want to travel, you hope to pass, you plan to move, you decide to change, you would like to start. Because the meaning is future-facing, the infinitive is the natural partner, and the pattern is completely regular — nothing changes except the first verb. Watch two things. “Would like” always takes an infinitive, never -ing: “I’d like to go”, not “I’d like going”. And a small set of verbs takes -ing instead, usually because they describe experiencing an activity rather than aiming at one: enjoy, finish, avoid, keep. Keeping those two lists apart is what stops sentences like “I hope going” or “I enjoy to travel”.

chart.title: Verb + infinitive for plans and wishes
rows: I want to travel next year.
I hope to finish by June.
We plan to move in July.

more: I’m going to start a new course in March.
I hope to work abroad one day.
I’d like to learn another language after English.
She plans to move next year.
I need to save some money first.
I decided not to change jobs this year.

fix.right: I hope to travel next year.
fix.why: “Hope” is followed by “to + verb”.

fix.right: I would like to study design.
fix.why: “Would like” always needs “to” before the verb.

fix.wrong: I plan to not work in August.
fix.right: I plan not to work in August.
fix.why: “Not” goes before “to”.

drill.name: Certainty ladder
drill.prompt: Say the same future idea at three levels: firm (“I’m going to…”), likely (“I plan to…”), distant (“I hope to…”).

dialogue.line: What are you going to do when the course finishes?
I’m going to take the B1 exam in June.
And after that?
I’d like to work abroad, and I hope to study something related to design.

contrast.title: How certain is the plan?
rows: I’m going to start in March.
I plan to / I need to
I hope to / I’d like to
I hope to start one day.

grammar.sound: “I’d like to” compresses to /aɪdlaɪktə/. The clue that it is “would like” and not “like” is the tiny /d/ — listen for it.

speaking.text: Then and now: describe your life five years ago and today, using “used to” and the present simple.
Interview your partner about three changes in their city. Ask follow-up questions in the past simple.
Future bingo: write six plans on a card. Find classmates who share them by asking “Are you going to…?”

tips: Exact past time → past simple. Result now → present perfect.
“Used to” only describes the past, never the present.
After hope, want, plan and would like, use “to + verb”.

quiz.q: My city ___ a lot in the last ten years.
quiz.explain: The change connects the past to now, so we use the present perfect: “has changed”.

dynamics.name: Then and now gallery
dynamics.how: Students post two lines on the wall: one “I used to…” and one “Now I…”. Everyone circulates, reads, and finds the three people whose changes are most similar to their own, then asks each a past-simple follow-up.
dynamics.payoff: Every learner produces the contrast, then hears it twenty more times.

dynamics.name: Tense triage
dynamics.how: Give twelve sentence stems with time expressions. Groups sort them into three piles — past simple, present simple, present perfect — and must justify any disagreement out loud.
dynamics.payoff: The justification is where the rule actually gets learned.

dynamics.name: Five-year interview
dynamics.how: Student A interviews B about five years ago, today and five years ahead — three questions each. B answers, then A reports two answers back to the class.
dynamics.payoff: All three time frames in one conversation, plus a reporting stage.

dynamics.name: Goal auction
dynamics.how: Each group has a budget and a list of twelve goals. They must buy four, defending each with a verb + infinitive sentence (“We need to…”, “We hope to…”).
dynamics.payoff: Forces variety across the infinitive verbs instead of repeating “want to”.

writing.title: Five years of change
writing.brief: Write two paragraphs. In the first, describe how your life or your city has changed in five years, using past simple, present simple and present perfect. In the second, describe three things you plan or hope to do next.
criteria: All three tenses appear and each is used for its own job.
At least one “used to” sentence about a habit that stopped.
Three different verb + infinitive patterns in the second paragraph.

homework.title: Course closing note
homework.task: Write a 120-word note to the version of yourself who started this course: what you couldn’t do then, what you can do now, and two goals for the next level. Read it aloud once and time yourself — aim for under ninety seconds.

test.q: My city ___ a lot in the last ten years.
test.explain: The change connects the past to now, so the present perfect is right.

test.q: I ___ take the bus, but now I walk.
test.explain: The positive form of the past habit is “used to”.
“Hope” is followed by “to + verb”.
A finished period with a date takes the past simple.
“Not” comes before “to” in a negative infinitive.

board: A three-part timeline: BEFORE — NOW — AFTER, with one model sentence on each.
Under BEFORE: past simple and “used to”. Under NOW: present simple. Bridging the two: present perfect.
A certainty ladder on the right: going to · plan to · want to · hope to · would like to.
A boxed model: “I used to take the bus, but now I walk. The city has changed a lot.”
Corner errors: “I have lived here in 2015” and “I hope travelling”.
